transcripts.text: If you're thinking about investing in Nvidia, TSMC, or perhaps RM, you need to know everything about the semi conductor space. Here's a crash course. First you need to understand that designing a semi conductor chip and actually building it are two totally different skill sets, which is why most companies focus only on one. The companies that manufacture the chips are called foundries. The biggest player here is the Taiwan Semi Conductor Manufacturing Company or TSMC with a 56% market share, followed by Samsung and Global Foundries with 12 and 6% market share respectively. The company designing chips are called fab less companies, which is short for fabrication less. They design the chips but don't make them. This includes big names like Invidia, AMD and Qualcomm who makes chips for iPhones. Big tech companies like Apple, Google, Amazon and Tesla are also in this group. A few companies like Samsung and Intel do both designing and making chips, but that's pretty rare these days. There are also companies like ARM that don't make or design chips, create and sell the designs to others. They only sell their IP. Lastly, some companies make the huge machines needed to manufacture semi conductors. These machines are as big as a bus and super expensive. Some cost up to $160 million. ASML is the top company in this field and their next generation of machines might cost up to $400 million. Follow for more.

transcripts.text: What's the difference between a CEO, CFO, and CEO? By my friend Nicholas Butcher. The CEO or chief executive officer leads the company. Their job is to create strategy, growth, and innovations that drive the company forward. They set the corporate values, they focus on client acquisition, they help to develop the brand, and they drive product development to ensure the company can grow. The CEO, or chief operating officer, is responsible for daily operations. The CEO implement the strategy and initiatives that are created by the CEO and is measured by the CFO. They focus on managing operational aspects of the business, they manage operational risk, and they coordinate product manufacturing, delivery, and service. text:
Margin vs. Markup

Knowing the difference can improve profits!

To calculate margin and markup, you need three numbers:

1: Revenue: Income earned from sales after discounts & rebates
2: Cost of Goods Sold (COGS): The cost to create the product/service
3: Gross Profit: Revenue - COGS

🔹 Margin is based on the selling price.

It shows the percentage of the selling price that becomes gross profit.

Formula: (Gross Profit / Reveue) x 100

🔹 Markup is calculated based on the cost.

It shows how much higher the selling price is than the item cost.

Formula: (Gross Profit / Cost of Goods Sold) x 100

Example!

You own a bike shop. You sell a bike for $200 that costs you $150. 

Margin: ($50 / $200) X 100 = 25%

Markup: ($50 / $150) x 100 = 33% 

Understanding the difference is crucial for pricing strategies, financial analysis, and overall business acumen.

#invesing #finance #accounting #accountingstudent

Revenue, that's the income you get from selling an item. Cost of good sold, which is the cost of the item that you're selling. And gross profit, which is simply revenue minus cost of good sold. So your margin is gross profit divided by revenue. This shows you for every dollar in sales, how many pennies you keep as gross profit. Markup shows you how much more your selling prices than the amount the item cost you to create. And the formula is gross profit divided by cost of good sold. And the third is through internally generated funds, which are when you reinvest profits generated in the company back into the business. All three funding sources end up on a company's balance sheet and increase the company's cash position. Debt and equity also impact the company's income statement because debt requires interest expense and equity increases the number of shares that are outstanding. Smart companies use a combination of debt, equity, and internally generated funds to fund projects and optimize return for investors. If visual summaries like this are useful, follow me for more.

If you want to undersatnd accounting, you must know debits and credits work. 

Here's a simplified breakdown:

Account Types and Their Normal Balances:

💰 Assets: Debit (Increased by Debit, Decreased by Credit)
💸 Expenses: Debit (Increased by Debit, Decreased by Credit)
📈 Dividend: Debit (Increased by Debit, Decreased by Credit)
📉 Losses: Debit (Increased by Debit, Decreased by Credit)

📊 Liabilities: Credit (Increased by Credit, Decreased by Debit)
💼 Capital: Credit (Increased by Credit, Decreased by Debit)
💵 Revenue: Credit (Increased by Credit, Decreased by Debit)
📈 Gains: Credit (Increased by Credit, Decreased by Debit)

Key Points to Remember:

• All Assets, Losses, and Expenditure accounts will have a Debit balance.
• All Liabilities, Gains, and Revenues accounts will have a Credit balance.
• All journal entries are placed in their respective ledger accounts.
• The first step in accounting is to pass a Journal Entry for every transaction.
• Some accounts will be debited and some will be credited.
 
Example:
In accounting, every transaction affects two accounts:

• Business makes a sale of $700 in cash
• Cash account is increased (debited) by $700.
• Revenue account is increased (credited) by $700.

transcripts.text: Balance sheet ratios every investor should know. First is the quick ratio. This answers the question can the company pay its bills? The equation here is cash and equivalents plus receivables divided by current liabilities. So cash and equivalents plus receivables divided by current liabilities. This number is below 1, that means the business is fragile. If this number is above 1.5, that's a really good sign for investors. Number two is the current ratio. This answers the question how well does the company manage its assets? The formula here is current assets divided by current liabilities. So current assets divided by current liabilities. If this number is below 0.7, that means the business is fragile. If it's over 2, that means the business is anti fragile. Next is the debt to equity ratio. This ratio answers the question how much leverage is the company using? The equation here is total liabilities divided by total shareholders equity. So total liabilities divided by total shareholders equity. If this number is above 2, that means there's more debt liabilities than equity and the business is fragile. If it's below 0.7, that means there's more equity than there is liabilities and the business is anti fragile. Finally is the goodwill to asset ratio, which answers the question is the company growing organically? The equation is goodwill divided by total assets. So goodwill divided by total assets. As a guide, if this number is over 50% the company is growing through acquisition and if This number is under 10%. The business is primarily growing organically.

Ever wonder how a public company’s organizational structure works? 

It typically follows a clear hierarchy—each tier has distinct powers and responsibilities.

Shareholders:

Roles: Provide capital, elect the Board of Directors, approve major decisions

Powers: Own equity stakes, influence long-term strategy through voting rights, and hold the Board accountable.

Board of Directors:

Roles: Set company direction, select and evaluate the CEO, ensure adherence to legal and regulatory standards.

Powers: Oversee executive compensation, approve strategic initiatives, and shape corporate governance policies.

Chief Executive Officer (CEO):

Roles: Lead the organization, implement Board-approved strategies, and ensure company-wide alignment with goals and values.

Powers: Make high-level decisions on operations, allocate resources, and guide the senior leadership team.

C-Suite Executives (e.g., CFO, COO, CMO, CTO):

Roles: Oversee specific functions (finance, operations, marketing, technology), manage budgets, and drive functional strategies.
Powers: Direct department initiatives, set performance targets, and influence policy within their domains.

Middle Management (Directors, Managers):

Roles: Translate high-level strategies into actionable plans, oversee projects and teams, ensure departmental performance and development.

Powers: Make day-to-day operational decisions, manage staff, and optimize resources to meet set objectives.

Employees (Frontline and Specialists):

Roles: Execute tasks, engage with customers, build products, and deliver services aligned with the company’s mission.

Powers: Influence quality and efficiency through their work, provide feedback up the chain, and represent the company’s brand in their daily interactions.

transcripts.text: Profit Drivers by Brian Faraldi there are three primary value triggers that can help to drive increased profit out of business. Value trigger No. 1 is sales. If we can increase sales by increasing the volume of units that we sold, we can increase our sales growth rate. This will increase profits. We can also improve our sales by focusing on price of the products that we sell or the mix of products that we sell. This can also lead to an increase in sales growth rate, which can increase our profits. Now, increasing sales can also help to drive operating leverage, where we're spreading our fixed costs out over a greater number of sales. This can help to drive our operating profit margin higher overtime, which can also improve our profits. Now, increasing sales can also give us economies of scale where we gain pricing power over our suppliers, thereby reducing our costs of good sold, which can increase our profit margin. The second value trigger is by focusing on operating costs, or the operating expenses taken on by the business. If we can take these costs out of the business, focusing on cost efficiencies, we can also increase our profit margin. Even if sales does not grow, this increases our profits overall. Finally, we can make investments in the business that help to drive profits higher. By focusing on investment and efficiencies, we can make investments in capital expenditures, property, plant, equipment that can either drive sales higher, Or our cost lower. It's important that if we're making these investments, that we get an incremental investment rate of return that exceeds our cost of capital. transcripts.text: Three types of income by Brian Feroldi. First is active income. This is income you gain through working. You're trading hours of your life for money. The second type is portfolio income. This is capital gains from financial assets such as stocks or bonds. This is when you put your money at risk in the hopes of generating capital gains from their appreciation. Third type is called passive income. This is cash flow from owning assets such as dividends received, royalties received, rent on real estate, and more. These are when the assets that you own produce income for you and put money into your pocket. If you're financially savvy, you should take your active income and try and convert it into both portfolio and passive income over time, eventually generating enough passive and portfolio income to replace your active income entirely. This does look fun, but there is a good rule to follow over here. If you don't have the ability to pay in full, you probably shouldn't be going. According to this article, it could cost anywhere between 2,500 to 7,000 dollars per person? Cause we're talking about $600 for general mission tickets. Hundred and fifty bucks for food and drinks. Even the Fed Chair Jerome Powell recently said that stocks are overvalued. So let's take a look at what we're looking at when we say stocks are overvalued. The Cape ratio or the Schiller PE ratio is looking at the prices against the inflation adjusted earnings from the last 10 years and it's sitting at a 25 year high. The only time higher was at the 2000 dot com bubble. And then we have the buffer indicator. This one simple. This looks at the total value to stock market against the GDP and this shows that the stock market is double the size of the GDP and it's sitting at all time high. text: Recent market sell-offs are largely driven by turmoil in Japan's financial markets, significantly impacting global investors engaged in the carry trade. With the Bank of Japan's negative interest rate policy, investors have been borrowing cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets abroad. However, shifts in Japanese monetary policy and rising global interest rates have led to sharp currency fluctuations and market volatility. This has forced investors to unwind their carry trades, resulting in widespread sell-offs and heightened market instability.

transcripts.text: Japan's Nikkei index plunged  more than 12% in a single day marking at the worst single  day drop in 37 years losing all of its gains  that it has made this  entire year so far the sell off was so bad this triggered circuit breakers halting trading for the entire market what had triggered this was the Bank of Japan  raising interest rates for  the second time since 2007 so why is that important? for the longest time Japan had near zero interest rates or even in fact negative interest rates meaning that you have to  pay interest to the bank  to deposit your money rather than the bank paying you interest but there was one advantage to that you as a consumer get to borrow really really cheap money  but that creates a really  interesting arbitrage opportunity because you as a consumer get to borrow really cheap yen  and invest that into  a higher producing area and then take those earnings repay that super cheap loan  that you got from here and then profit  that is what we call a Carry Trade but people will inevitably lever up meaning that they borrow a boatload so when that super cheap loan  that they got becomes not as super cheap they get something called a margin call meaning that they have  to pay back the loan but in order to do so  they have to sell their stuff over here which is causing this cascading  domino effect that is  impacting the US markets crypto markets and everything I wouldn't be surprised if volatility  continues for next few weeks so if you wanna stay updated on what  I'm buying and selling in real time make sure to check out the Blossom app linked in my bio they're completely free or comment the word    INVEST and I'll send it to you directly

By following the Cheri Method, you can effectively manage your paycheck, ensuring that you are saving for the future, investing wisely, paying down debt, and covering essential expenses.

🚨 Recession Warning: A key economic indicator just flashed red!
📉 The Inverted Yield Curve: This signal has historically predicted recessions with high accuracy.
⚠️ What It Means: When short-term bonds (3-month) pay more interest than long-term bonds (10-year), it's a sign of economic trouble ahead.
🔄 How It Works: Investors anticipating a recession buy more long-term bonds, driving prices up and interest rates down.
🏦 Why It Matters: Every time this pattern reversed in the past, a recession followed shortly after.

Here is how I would invest  my first $1000 if I was a beginner first I'd open up my brokerage app of choice I am using RobinHood as they are the hands down most  user friendly app available on the market if you are interested in signing up I do have a referral link in my bio where if you sign up you will get a free stock but use any app of your choice my first pick will be VTI which is the Vanguard Total Stock Market Index this is essentially basically investing into everything because over time the  whole stock market will go up and so instead of picking and choosing it's good to have everything so I'll be putting in $300 into this my second choice will be IVV which is essentially the S&P 500 ETF and some might be wondering  why not just pick SPY as they are the most well known  S&P 500 ETF out there and that's because SPY  has a higher expense ratio than IVV for essentially the same exact exposure so over here I'll also be putting in $300 so we're at $600 total my 3rd pick will be QQQ  which is the tech heavy NASDAQ ETF tech has historically been more volatile however with more risk comes with higher return since I am young with a longer time  horizon and my risk tolerance is very high I'm willing to have that exposure so I'll be putting in $200 into here my next pick will be VWO which is the emergent market ETF it's good to have a diversified portfolio  and to have international exposure so I'll be putting in $100 into here my next choice will be VOE which is the Vanguard Mid Cap Value ETF I'll be putting in $50 into here and my very last choice will be VBR which is the Vanguard Small Cap Value ETF and I'll also be putting in $50 into here as well there you have it now I've built a well suitable diversified portfolio  that suits my risk tolerance this is not financial advice and everyone's financial goals  and situations are different so this might not apply to you but if you found this helpful please do me a favor drop a like hit that follow text:
The stock market may be in a bubble. The S&P 500 have gained about 15% for the first half of 2024 however only 10 companies out of the 500 have contributed about 77% of the entire markets gains. The remaining 490 stocks contributed the remaining 23%. To make it even worse, Nvidia alone has contributed about 34% of the markets gain. So one company has contributed more than 490 stocks. 

This rally can definitely continue however I am getting a bit cautious. I will be diversifying away slightly into other areas such as Chinese stocks. I’ve recently added a new position to my portfolio $KWEB since Chinese tech stocks look cheap

text:
How to invest $10k if you’re in your 50s. 

The asset allocation for someone in their 50s will look drastically different than someone who is younger as it should be a bit more conservative given that retirement is closer. This is leaning closer to the classic 60/40 portfolio but not quite there. 
These are my own opinion on how to build a portfolio for those in their 50s and not financial advice.

$2k - VOO: Tracks the S&P 500, offering diversified exposure to large-cap U.S. companies. 
$2k - SCHD: Focuses on high-quality dividend-paying U.S. stocks, adding income and stability.
$2k - QQQ: Invests in the Nasdaq-100, capturing tech growth potential even in your 50s.
$2k - AGG: A broad U.S. bond market ETF that provides core fixed-income exposure for stability.
$1k - BNDX: Gives access to international investment-grade bonds to diversify interest rate and currency risk.
$500 - PDBC: A commodity ETF that helps hedge inflation through exposure to physical assets like oil and metals.
$500 - IBIT: Offers Bitcoin exposure in an ETF format, adding a small but modern growth tilt to your portfolio.

text: President Trump escalates his feud with Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, demanding his termination for not cutting interest rates swiftly enough. Powell emphasizes the Fed’s independence and patience in navigating economic uncertainty, while Trump’s social media attacks intensify market volatility.

text:
Here’s how any college graduate can become a millionaire without trying.

Its commonly thought that you need a high paying job to get wealthy

That is farthest from the truth. You need need discipline and consistency

The average graduation age is 22. The average retirement age is 66. Thats 44 years 

If you simply invest $94/month, you will end up as a millionaire by the time you retire. 

Thats only $3.13/day

Most people pay more in coffee everyday.

text:
This is what you should do with your money every time to get paid

1. Direct deposited into a checking account - this will hold just enough money for short term expenses such as rent, utilities, credit card bills, etc. Any excess funds should go into 
2. High Yield Savings Account (HYSA) - make sure to get a good HYSA that pays 4% or more. Also make sure theres no fees and it’s FDIC insured. I have a list of some of the best and my personal favorites HYSA in my bio. Comment “BANK” and I’ll send you the list
3. Roth IRA - Contribute the maximum amount of $7000. You can still contribute to 2024 until April 15th. Make sure to invest the money after you deposit the funds into your Roth IRA. I would personally invest it into VOO, QQ, SCHD, IBIT, ETHA
4. Taxable Brokerage - if you maxed out your Roth IRA then contribute to your taxable brokerage. I have referrals in my bio for some amazing sign up bonuses like up to 30 free stocks when signing up using the link in my bio.

The left gather the highest number of deputies followed by the President party and by the far-right.

transcripts.text: So French President Macron lost everything yesterday. French people elected their new deputies and the president lost his majority. But it's actually messier than you think. About a month ago, French President Emmanuel Macron dissolved the National Assembly, which is the US House of representatives equivalent. But he only gave less than one month for a new election to take place. In France, there are three major blocks the far right, the center, which is the president block and more right leaning, and the left, which is usually broken down into many parties going from center left, far left. The president wanted more deputies because he previously didn't have the majority, but it didn't work as planned. The left united into a single party and gained most of the votes, followed by the far right, and Emmanuel Macron's party came in the third position. In France, the president must usually use the majority party to pick his prime minister and ministers and constitute his government. But now the three major parties are split almost evenly and none of them have the majority to govern the state. The left is leading, but could potentially break apart between center and far left again. If no alliance is made between different parties, the country could be grid locked for a while. The president has a one year cooldown to dissolve the National Assembly again.

transcripts.text: So the market will crash when the Fed cuts rates in September? In case you missed it, the Fed chairman Jerome Powell said it was time to lower interest rates in a speech last week at Jackson Hole, giving us a strong hint that this will happen at the next Fed meeting on September 18th. Many believe this could cause the next market crash because when you look at past data, most crisis happens when the Fed starts lowering rates. On the flip side, some argue that lower rates will make money more available and should therefore boost the economy. So which of this is correct? Here's the rule of thumb. If the Fed start to cut because the economy is weak, the market tends to react negatively and they expect the economy to get worse on the short term. However, if the Fed cut preventively to avoid an economic crisis, the market can see that positively and go higher. The major problem right now is that we don't know the real state of the job market. Even the Fed doesn't trust the job numbers anymore, so it's difficult to know where we are exactly. The third scenario is if the market already expects a rate cut, it might have already adjusted. When the cut comes, nothing could happen. In the short term at least.

transcripts.text: So the trade war is escalating again, but this time the U. S. Is not involved. China just announced major retaliatory tariffs on Canada, who previously imposed 100% tariffs on Chinese made electric cars on October 1st last year, following the footsteps of the U S. And EU. Few weeks later on October 15th, Canada imposed another tariff of 25% on steel and aluminum products from China. China fought back today with a retaliatory tariff of 100% on Canadian rapeseed oil, oil cakes and peas and a 25% tariff on aquatic products and pork, saying Canada's unilateral decision to impose tariff goes against the World Trade Organization rules. However, some suggest the timing is also a warning shot against the Trump administration who paused tariff on Canada and Mexico but not on China. According to Jerome Powell, who spoke at the university of Chicago Booth School of business forum yesterday, there is a lot of uncertainty on how tariffs will impact inflation. However, he said Trump trade tariffs in its first term were far from being inflationary, but caused global growth to slow and actually LED the Fed to cut interest rates.

transcripts.text: So here's the main economic events of December 1st. On December 12th and 13, we have the biggest economic event of the month, the next Fed meeting at which they will decide whether to raise interest rates or not. We already know what will happen with a high degree of certainty, as 97% of traders are betting on no rate hikes. Jerome Powell will speak on the 13th, providing an update on the feds views and concerns regarding inflation. The FOMC minutes, which detail the discussions of this meeting will be released about three weeks later in January. Also on December 12th, the Consumer Price Index, or CPI, will be released, providing data on inflation. Following this, on December 13th, the Producer Price Index, CPI will be released, offering insights into inflation at the wholesale level. Then on December 22nd, the Personal Consumption Expenditures, PCE will be released, which provides inflation data similar to the CPI. Additionally, the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey will be out on December 5th. However, the Fed has indicated that it is not focusing as heavily on the job market for its decision making process currently. Keep in mind that all the numbers released in December actually reflect the data from November. If you wanna see daily financial news, follow for more.

If you do more than 4 times that is when you will be charged right so perhaps in the next video I'm going to explain what emergency savings is all about there are also some investments that you can do on Piggyvest platform They have the Investify, Corporate debt note as well that opens up from time to time on Piggyvest right so you can download the app on the Play Store or App Store the next is Risevest yes with Risevest, you can invest in real estate yes in dollars you can invest in stocks, you can do fixed deposits and then you can save as well on Risevest but you're better off doing real estate investment or doing what's it called fixed investment rather than just saving because the interest that you get on the real estate or the fixed investment or the stock is much better off than just saving on Risevest and just like Bamboo, you don't need a dorm account right your naira is going to be converted to dollar at the prevailing exchange rate yeah it is going to be converted at the prevailing exchange rate on the platform. The next one is Trove, Trove is a platform that allows you to invest in US stocks, ETFs, and local stocks. So, you see like you literally have no excuse for not starting your investment journey because these are apps that are available at your finger tips. So, if you have a smartphone with internet go to Playstore and App store you can also check out their website to read more on them, the different regulations with SEC, CBN and all the likes that they have and then you go ahead to start investing right away and you know like I usually say that you don't need millions of naira before you start investing with your 5,000 naira, you can begin your investment journey Like I mention that with $1, $5, $10 you can start investing in US stocks, in ETFs on Bamboo or Trove as the case may be. So, there you go top investment apps that is available for you to start investing I want to hear from you in the comment section which one do you want to start researching on this week and start making plans to start investing with them or saving with them literally you have no excuse still saving in your traditional bank account imagine a 1 to 5% per annum compared to 22, getting free money without stress just because you are saving or just because you are investing right. Another app I forgot to mention is the FSDH app. The FSDH app allows you to invest in mutual fund I personally do FSDH mutual fund so you are able to invest in mutual fund on the FSDH app right. So, you see there are tons of app and this is not get rich quick scheme anything these apps, a number of them are regulated by SEC and CBN so you have nothing to worry about majority or let me say all of this app is going to request for your BVN so you have nothing to worry about and please ensure that you do your proper due diligence as well. If you think that your heart or whatever is not going with any of the app it's okay, it's not compulsory that you download all the apps on your account and yeah start investing on all of them, no, it is not compulsory that you have all the apps. Do your research, do your due diligence and select the ones that aligns with your financial goal right and start investing with them. So, there you have it, the top investment apps if you think I forgot anyone please drop it in the comment section and I'm going to say one or two things about it. If you enjoyed this video, you found it educative, interesting, and inspiring don't forget to like, share, follow for more tips on building wealth and I will see you in my next video cheers.

text: Here's what would happen if Trump forces the Fed to cutinterest rates by 3%.

authorMeta.name: quarterchart
authorMeta.signature: Check companies long term trend easily and make faster investing decisions with

transcripts.text: So here's what would happen if the Fed lowered interest rates by 3% today. Trump wants Jerome Powell to lower the interest rates immediately by 300 basis points from 4.5% to 1.5% in order to stimulate the economy and lower the interest rates the US pays on its debt. Right now the U. S. Government has a yearly deficit of 1.8 trillion dollars but it spends roughly 900 billion paying the interest on its debt. So the theory is if the Fed cuts deep, the government could refinance its debt with a lower interest rate and therefore reduce its deficit massively. However, in practice, it's more difficult for two main reasons. First, even if interest rates are low across the board, the U. S. Government needs to find buyers to refinance the $37 trillion of debt which is going to be difficult especially when it puts a tariff on every country. Second, the Fed interest rate is actually the overnight interest rate. Even if they bring it to 0% it will lower the Treasuries with a low maturity like 2 years or less but won't have as much impact on 10 years or more. We could even see the 30 year Treasury rising if the market thinks lowering interest rates is bad long term. If you want to lower the back end of the curve, you need to do quantitative easing when the Fed buys bonds directly on the market which is kind of like printing money. But basically if Trump can convince The market that his strategy will work and the US manages to refinance a big chunk of its debt at much lower interest rates, it could help reduce the deficit and put the country in a better position long term. On the flip side, cutting rates too much could lead to more inflation and make investors worry that the US is just kicking the can down the road. That could hurt trust in the dollar and make borrowing more expensive in the future. What do you think will happen?

text:
How to analyze an income statement
Ask these 11 questions:
1: Does revenue consistently grow?
→Analyzing revenue trends over time can help assess the company's growth and stability.
2: What is the gross margin?
→Gross margin, which is gross profit divided by revenue, indicates how efficiently the company manages its production costs.
3: Is the gross margin stable? Expanding? Contracting? Why?
→Changes in the gross margin trend provide insights into the company's pricing power with consumers and cost control measures with suppliers.
4: Are there research + development expenses?
→Research & Development expenses indicate the company's has to continuously innovate to drive future growth.
5: Are there selling + marketing expenses?
→Big selling and marketing expenses indicate the company has to spend heavily to promote its products or services.
6: What are the company's biggest operating expenses?
→Identifying the biggest expense, such as labor or cost of goods sold, can pinpoint the areas where cost management is critical.
7: What is the company's operating margin?
→Operating margin, which is operating profit divided by revenue, measures how efficient a company is at converting revenue into profits.
8: Does the company have any non-operating expenses?
→Looking for non-operating expenses like interest payments or one-time charges is essential for understanding the impact of financial activities outside the company's core operations.
9: What is the company's net profit margin?
→Net profit margin, which is net profit divided by revenue, indicates the overall profitability of the company after all expenses.
10: Is the company profitable on a Non-GAAP basis?
→Looking at non-GAAP profitability enables you tp understand if the company's profit picture differs when certain accounting adjustments are made.
11: Is the company profitable on a GAAP basis?
→Assessing profitability on a Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) basis provides insight into whether the company complies with standard accounting rules and is profitable within that framework.

Asset vs. Equity
Assets are what the company owns and uses to generate income. 
Equity is what’s left for the owners after debts are paid.

Current Asset vs. Fixed Asset
Current Assets are short-term resources (like cash, inventory) used within a year.
Fixed Assets (like buildings, machinery) are long-term and not easily converted to cash.
Easy reminder: Current = <1 year; Fixed = +1 year.

Accounts Receivable vs. Accounts Payable
Accounts Receivable: Money owed to you by customers. 
Accounts Payable: Money you owe suppliers.
Easy reminder: Receivable = Receive; Payable = Pay.

Depreciation vs. Amortization
Depreciation applies to tangible assets (like equipment) losing value over time. Amortization applies to intangible assets (like patents).
Easy reminder: D for Desks (physical); A for Abstractions (intangible).

Market Value vs. Book Value
Market Value is what someone’s willing to pay today 
Book Value is what the balance sheet says the asset is worth.
Easy reminder: Market = Real price; Book = Paper price.

Gross Profit vs. Gross Margin

📚 Grab my FREE accounting infographic ebook (link in bio)

To differentiate between gross profit and gross margin, you need two numbers:
Revenue: Income from sales after discounts & rebates.
Cost of Goods Sold (COGS): The cost to produce the product/service.
🔹 Gross Profit is the dollar amount of profit after covering the cost of goods sold.
Formula: Gross Profit = Revenue - COGS

🔹 Gross Margin is the percentage of revenue that becomes gross profit.
Formula: (Gross Profit / Revenue) x 100

Example
You run a bakery. You sell a cake for $40 that costs $25 to make.
Gross Profit: $40 - $25 = $15
Gross Margin: ($15 / $40) x 100 = 37.5%
Why It Matters:
Gross profit tells you how much cash you make from each sale, while gross margin shows the efficiency of your cost structure. Understanding both helps with pricing, cost control, and profitability strategies.

Apple Net Income vs Free Cash Flow

They are NOT the same thing!

Here's the difference:
💰 NET INCOME
🔎 FOUND ON: Income Statement
🔢 ACCOUNTING: Accrual
➗ FORMULA: Revenue - Expenditures = Net Income
Net income measures a company’s profitability on the income statement using accrual accounting.
It shows how much profit a company earned in theory during the period.
It's an accountant's opinion of profit. Net Income can be easily manipulated.
💰 FREE CASH FLOW
🔎 FOUND ON: Cash Flow Statement
🔢 ACCOUNTING: Cash
➗ FORMULA: Operating Cash Flow - Capital Expenditures = Free Cash Flow
Free cash flow measures the actual cash flow available to shareholders on the cash flow statement using cash accounting.
It shows how much cash was generated by the company during the period.
Free cash flow is much harder to manipulate than Net Income.
Remember: Net Income is an opinion. Free Cash Flow is a fact.
Both numbers are important, but when forced to choose, I'll take free cash flow every time.
•Net Income = accounting profit based on all reported income/expenses.
•Free Cash Flow = actual cash left after essentials, showing real liquidity.
In short, net income is what’s on paper, free cash flow is what’s in the bank!

transcripts.text: Three depreciation methods explained by Brian Feroleto. So depreciation is the accounting method of spreading out the cost of a tangible asset over its useful life. So tangible just means something you can physically touch, like a car, equipment or a building. Now method No. 1 is called the straight line depreciation. This is the most common and the easiest method. You take the cost of the item and divide it by its useful life. So if something costs a hundred thousand dollars and it's expected to last five years, that's a 20 thousand dollar depreciation each year. Method No. 2 is called the declining balance method, and this is used to calculate large depreciation expenses or assets that quickly lose value. So you take the opening book value, hundred thousand dollars, and you multiply that by the depreciation rate. Now the depreciation rate is 100% divided by the total useful life of the asset. In this case, the asset's life is five years. So 100% divided by five years is 20%. So we take 20% off of the value of the asset each year. The final method is called the sum of the year digits. This is an accelerated depreciation method that takes most of the expenses in the early years and less in the latter years. You take the total cost of the item, hundred thousand dollars, and then you multiply that by the useful life year divided by the sum of the year digits. So 1 2 3 4 5. That's 15. So the depreciation rate in year one is 5 5 divided by 15 is 33%. In year two it's 4 divided by 15. So the depreciation is 26,000. In year three it's 3 divided by 15, So this takes a much bigger depreciation in the earlier years and less depreciation in the out years. If this type of analysis is helpful, follow me for more.

AMORTIZATION 📜
An accounting method used to write down the value of intangible assets (such as patents, copyrights, and trademarks) that have a finite useful life. It's the process of expensing the cost of an intangible asset over its estimated useful life.
Amortization happens to INTANGIBLE Assets (you CAN'T touch them)
Examples:
→Copyrights 📰
→Loans 💰
→Patents 👨‍⚖️
DEPRECIATION 🚗
An accounting method used to allocate the cost of tangible assets (such as buildings. machinery, and vehicles) over their useful lives. It represents the systematic reduction in the value of an asset due to wear and tear, obsolescence, or other factors.
Depreciation happens to TANGIBLE Assets (you CAN touch them)
Examples:
→Car 🚘
→Equipment 🤖
→Buildings 🏭
FINANCIAL STATEMENT IMPACT:
Amortization is recorded on the income statement, reducing net income. The contra-asset account accumulated amortization is created on the balance sheet, being the portion of the intangible asset that has been used up.
Depreciation is recorded on the income statement, reducing the company's net income. Simultaneously, an equal amount is recorded as an accumulated depreciation contra-asset account on the balance sheet.

How to analyze a balance sheet in <2 minutes:

Answer these 12 questions:

1: How much cash does the company have?
✅ Best possible Answer: More cash than debt.

2: Are there accounts receivables? How much?
✅ Best possible Answer: None. This means the company is paid in cash.

3: Is there inventory? How much?
✅ Best possible Answer: None. This means the company doesn't have to worry about managing inventory.

4: Is there any goodwill? How much?
✅ Best possible Answer: None. This means the company has grown organically.

5: What are the company's biggest assets?
✅ Best possible Answer: Cash. This means the company has plenty of financial flexibility.

6: Does the company have debt? How much? What kind?
✅ Best possible Answer: None. This means the company hasn't financed itself with debt.

7: Does the company have deferred revenue?
✅ Best possible Answer: Yes. It's a sign that the company gets paid before it delivers the product/service.

8: What are the company's biggest liabilities?
✅ Best possible Answer: Deferred revenue. See question 7.

9: How has the company been funded? Debt? Equity?
✅ Best possible Answer: Equity. This means the company is free of debt.

10: Is there any preferred stock?
✅ Best possible Answer: No. Preferred stock is a sign that a company has poor economics.

11: Are retained earnings positive and growing?
✅ Best possible Answer: Yes. This means the company is profitable and retains its profits for growth.

12: Is there any treasury stock?
✅ Best possible Answer: Yes. This means the company is buying back stock.

text:
Accrued Revenue vs. Deferred Revenue – What’s the Difference?

👉 FOLLOW @brianferoldi for more content like this.

If you’ve ever looked at a company’s financial statements, you may have noticed two interesting items: accrued revenue and deferred revenue. Although they sound similar, they represent opposite sides of the revenue recognition process.

1. Accrued Revenue

What It Is: Revenue that’s been earned but not yet invoiced or received.
Example: You’ve delivered a consulting project this month, but you won’t invoice (and get paid) until next month. You still recognize the revenue in the month you provided the service.

Why It Matters: Accrued revenue ensures you’re accurately reflecting the revenue you’ve generated—even before cash changes hands.

2. Deferred Revenue

What It Is: Cash received in advance for goods or services that haven’t been delivered yet.

Example: A software company bills customers upfront for a 12-month subscription. The cash is in the bank, but the company can’t record it as revenue until each month’s service is delivered.

Why It Matters: Deferred revenue appears as a liability on the balance sheet, reminding you that you owe products or services in the future.

Key Takeaways:

Timing is everything – Accrued revenue reflects work already done, while deferred revenue shows payment received before the work is complete.

Cash vs. Recognition – Accrued revenue helps match earnings with the period of performance; deferred revenue prevents prematurely recognizing income.

Financial Planning – Understanding these concepts helps you monitor cash flows, manage working capital, and maintain compliance with accounting standards.

By keeping a close eye on accrued and deferred revenue, you’ll have a clearer picture of your company’s financial health—and be better equipped to plan for growth.

text:
Bookkeeping vs. Accounting – What’s the Difference?

👉 FOLLOW @brianferoldi for more content like this.

While the two terms are often used interchangeably, bookkeeping and accounting serve different (but equally important) roles in managing a business’s finances.

Bookkeeping
Primary Focus: Recording day-to-day financial transactions.
Tasks Involved: Keeping track of sales, receipts, invoices, and payments; updating ledgers and reconciling bank statements.
Key Benefit: Provides the foundation of accurate data on which all financial analysis is built.
Accounting
Primary Focus: Interpreting, classifying, analyzing, summarizing, and reporting financial data.
Tasks Involved: Creating financial statements, budgeting, tax planning, and strategic financial decision-making.
Key Benefit: Offers insights that guide business strategy, ensuring regulatory compliance and long-term growth.
Why It Matters:
Without good bookkeeping, you’re left with messy, unreliable data—making it tough to see the real financial picture.
Without solid accounting, you miss critical insights that can save money, improve cash flow, and steer your company toward success.

transcripts.text: What's the difference between a budget and a forecast? By Brian Feroldi. A budget is a financial plan that outlines revenue expectations, expenses, and goals for a specific period, usually a year. A budget sets financial targets and provides a baseline for resource allocations and performance expectations. Budget is relatively fixed once it's approved and it's used as a performance benchmark. It's only revised if major events occur. Budgets are highly detailed with line by line specificity, and teams are held accountable to meet their targets. A forecast is a rolling estimate of future performance and it's adjusted periodically based on actual results. Forecasts reflect up to date insights on outcomes and are used for proactive decision making. Forecasts are often shorter term in nature, like monthly, quarterly, and they are rolled forward. Forecasts have a lot of flexibility to them and they can change frequently based on new information. Forecasts are high level, so they're not very detailed and they're used for iterative adjustments rather than strict accountability measures. A Roth IRA is a retirement account where you contribute after-tax dollars. The big benefit? Your money grows tax-free, and withdrawals in retirement are also tax-free! 💸

You can withdraw your contributions anytime, tax and penalty-free. No other retirement account offers that kind of flexibility!

Here’s a step-by-step tutorial on how I’m planning to buy 100 shares of Nvidia at a lower price and get paid $200 👀
This strategy is called selling cash-secured puts, and it’s one Warren Buffett uses:
1. Pick a stock you're okay owning 100 shares of: In this case, I’m going with Nvidia.
2. Click on Trade > Trade Options: This opens the options menu.
3. Choose an expiration 30-45 days away: Make sure your toggles are set to *Sell* and *Put.* Since I want to buy Nvidia at $100, I’ll select that strike price.
4. Sell 1 contract and collect a premium: In this case, I'll get paid about $230. Here’s how it plays out:
- If Nvidia stays above $100 by expiration, I keep the $230 and don’t have to buy the shares.
- If Nvidia falls below $100, I’ll buy 100 shares at $100 each *and* keep the $230 premium.
Once I own 100 shares, I can start selling covered calls for even more income.
-Steve

7. Healthcare Planning: Plan for potential healthcare costs, including long-term care insurance, which can help protect your savings. 
8. Maximize Social Security: Develop a strategy for when to claim Social Security benefits to maximize your lifetime benefit. 

Taking these steps can help you build a secure financial future and enjoy a comfortable retirement.

Number one find an idea. There are several ways to do that, but the best one for beginners is just copy something that already works. This way you make sure that it's already validated and you have a much higher chance of success. Differentiate your app as you build it. No. 2 build it with A. I. Cool thing is nowadays you don't need to know coding to build an app. You can let A. I. Do most of the work for you. Here's the tech stack. I recommend cursor as your I. D. E, next JS and Chad C N as your frameworks, super base for backend and off stripe for payments and Vercel to deploy. No. 3 market it. The best way to market it is by creating content. Start by writing posts in communities where your target audience hangs out. Then start building an audience on a platform like TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, or X. Study other content that goes viral and try to recreate it. Finally, start an affiliate network to scale your content.

transcripts.text: AI is never going to replace investment bankers AI is also never going to replace private equity associates or accountants and anyone that does try to tell you that AI is going to replace those jobs either has less than one year of real experience in either of those fields or they're trying to sell you a product that is dependent on you handing over your free will to think critically and this is coming from a strategic finance professional who literally uses AI every single day for my job and you know the problem with these hyperbolic marketing driven assertions is that one it greatly understates the amount of complexity that actually goes into valuation work and two it makes a set of misguided assumptions about the economy at large in order for it to be true that AI can replace investment bankers or PE investors for example in the first place where this idea starts to blow up a little bit is around the concept of valuation and not just valuation in a vacuum but valuation and how it fits into a M&A transaction deal process if we're going to assume that AI can replace investment bankers we must also assume that AI is able to 1 handle valuation on its own end to end and 2 that valuation is a purely economically rational event 100% of the time the problem with that is that valuation is not inherently rational the value of a company is not some irrefutable truth in the same way that 2 plus two is irrefutably equal to four in fact the value of a company itself is simply equal to the highest price that someone else is willing to pay for it if no one else is willing to pay for your company the valuation of that company is zero and on the other hand a buyer's willingness to pay for an asset is purely driven by perception the perception of what you might say well the perception of all of the future free cash flows that this company is going to generate that's available to me as an equity investor at some point in the future discounted back to today's dollars even more simply said if I'm a buyer and I expect more cash from you in the future I'm willing to pay a higher price for that today if I expect less from you in the future I'm willing to pay a lower price for that today and then on the other hand you have the seller who is not going to accept a price today that doesn't accurately capture the value that they can achieve from their own expectations of the future both of these futures do not exist and this is the reason why people say that valuation is both a art and a science because past a certain point valuation is no longer a historical analysis of your operating performance as a company and determining what that is worth today it becomes an argument on what's going to happen into the future and what we can expect based on your historical performance and it is for this reason that investment bankers will present the value of the company in the form of a range across a variety different forms of valuation methodologies and it is that range of value that is up for discussion or really negotiation between buyer and seller in an M&A transaction process that's why I always say Valuation is not just a product of historical financial analysis it's also a product of mythmaking about a future that doesn't exist it's not just a product of you know extreme mathematical rigor it's also a product of human psychology and persuasion valuation and by proxy M&A is a process that must be uniquely facilitated by human agents because at the end of the day the price that someone is willing to pay for a company is never solely determined by the tangible value of the assets that they have today that they can see with their own eyes there's also the role of expectation of a future gain in which two parties have to come together and agree upon what the future is going to look like and decide how much that future is worth that is a truth that is not set in stone it is up for discussion AI on the other hand in my opinion works best when there is an operative truth that is irrefutable and some process or rationale on top of that operative truth that needs to be replicated or analyzed at scale now to be clear I do think that AI will play an extremely pivotal role in transforming the finance and financial services industry I just fundamentally believe that the transformation will come from making employees more efficient or more productive rather than ripping and replacing them all together like you should be using AI to upskill you tutor you teach you new things or you know improve your research process but no I don't think it's going to take your job anytime soon

transcripts.text: I've lost over 11 thousand dollars trading options. However, in the past month alone, I've made over 14 dollars trading options. By changing two things about my strategy. Originally, a lot of what I was doing was really just throwing money at different things and playing uh, earnings announcements. And so if I believe the price is gonna go up or the price is gonna go down, I was playing just earnings announcements. And that's uh, not very a good a good strategy, at least long term. One of the biggest changes that I made was buying call options that had a further expiration date. So for example, instead of buying a call option that expired in a give the week or in the next couple of days, I started to buy options that expired in the next couple of months. One of the primary ways I was going about this was I invest. I have a significant portfolio that is heavily weighted towards technology. Um, one of my investments is QQQ. With my belief that the value of QQQ was going to rise, I would I started to buy call options on QQQ with expiration dates going further out into October and and further than that as well. And what I found through this was that I was able to make money as a stock market rose. Because not only was I making money on my investments in QQQ, but I was also making money on the call options. That I purchased on QQQ. Additionally, with earnings announcements, I didn't stop trading on an earnings. But what I started to do, instead of just buying a call or put, I started to use straddle, which is a strategy where you're buying a call and a put with the same expiration date in the same price. And so this allows you basically to capture risks such that whether the price goes up or down, you stand to make money. If there is a large swing. Now, if there's a small swing, um, and the stock does not move that much either up or down, then you will lose a significant amount of money, which I've also experienced. See the 10 year minus 3 month curve has been deeply inverted since October of 2022, but now it's uninverting. When the 10 year minus 3 month curve uninverts, it typically marks the beginning of the end of the economy's expansion. This happens because short term interest rates remain elevated while long term rates start to fall reflecting a shift in investor sentiment towards slower growth or even contraction in the future. Essentially, bond investors are betting that the Fed will soon be forced to cut rates to combat a weakening economy and a weakening job market. This pattern was seen ahead of the recessions in 1989, 2001, signalling that the soft landing narrative was wishful thinking. And historically, markets don't wait for the recession to officially start and stocks often experience significant drawdowns before the recession is even announced. So although it's never a good idea to panic, I think this would be a good time to lock in some profits from overvalued stocks and sit in some cash.

First you need to understand that designing a semi conductor chip and actually building it are two totally different skill sets, which is why most companies focus only on one. The companies that manufacture the chips are called foundries. The biggest player here is the Taiwan Semi Conductor Manufacturing Company or TSMC with a 56% market share, followed by Samsung and Global Foundries with 12 and 6% market share respectively. The company designing chips are called fab less companies, which is short for fabrication less. They design the chips but don't make them. This includes big names like Nvidia, AMD and Qualcomm who makes chips for iPhones. Big tech companies like Apple, Google, Amazon and Tesla are also in this group. A few companies like Samsung and Intel do both designing and making chips, but that's pretty rare these days. There are also companies like ARM that don't make or design chips, create and sell the designs to others. They only sell their IP. Lastly, some companies make the huge machines needed to manufacture semi conductors. These machines are as big as a bus and super expensive. Some cost up to $160 million. ASML is the top company in this field and their next generation of machines might cost up to $400 million. And if you like this kind of video, share it with a friend.

text:
Fixed Assets vs Current Assets

Know the difference!

FIXED ASSETS 🚗 🏭 🤖 

Meaning: Tangible assets expected to benefit the company for 1+ years

Time Period: More than 1 year

Also Called: Long-term assets

Depreciation: Charged against these types of assets over time (except land)

Liquidity: Hard to convert to cash

Purpose: To grow the business and provide a competitive advantage

Financed: With long-term liabilities

CURRENT ASSETS 💰 💳 💲 

Meaning: Assets expected to be used or utilized in <1 year

Time Period: Less than 1 year

Also Called: Short-term assets

Depreciation: Not charged against these types of assets

Liquidity: Easy to convert to cash

Purpose: Running the business and funding short-term needs

Financed: With short-term liabilities

Follow Brian Feroldi  for more content like this.

#accounting #accountingstudent #finance #finance101 #investing #investingforbeginners

transcripts.text: What's the difference between a fixed asset and a current asset? By Brian Ferelli. Fixed asset is a tangible asset that's expected to benefit the company for more than one year. It's also called a long term asset. Now, fixed assets are depreciated over time, so they lose value except for land, and from a liquidity perspective, they are hard to convert to cash. Now, fixed assets are used to grow the business, create a competitive advantage, and they're typically financed with long term liabilities. Current assets are any assets that are expected to be used or utilized in less than one year, and they're also called short term assets. Now, current assets do not depreciate and they're very easy to convert to cash. Their purpose is to run the business and fund short term needs. Current assets are financed with short term liabilities such as payables, recruit expenses, and short term debt. If this type of analysis is useful, follow me for more.

💰 EBITDA
Stands for: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization
It is often used to evaluate a company's operating performance. It focuses on the business's core operations, excluding the effects of financing and accounting decisions.
💰 FCF
Stands for Free Cash Flow
It is the cash a company generates after accounting for cash outflows to support operations and maintain its capital assets.
💡PURPOSE
→ EBITDA: provides a view of a company's operational efficiency by excluding non-operating expenses.
→ FCF: reveals how much cash is available for dividends, debt repayment, and reinvestment after covering all expenses, including CapEx.
🎢 USAGE
→ EBITDA is often used by investors to compare companies within the same industry without the effects of financing and accounting decisions.
→ FCF is crucial for assessing a company's ability to generate cash and fund growth, repurchase stock, pay dividends, and reduce debt.
🔢 CALCULATION
EBITDA
➡ Operating Income + Depreciation + Amortization
FCF
➡ Cash Flow From Operations - Capital Expenditures
Each metric serves a unique purpose in financial analysis, and each offers valuable insights for investors, managers, and stakeholders.

text:
Warren Buffett’s Income Statement Rules of Thumb:

1: Gross Margin
🧮 Equation: Gross Profit / Revenue
👍 Rule of Thumb: 40% or higher
🤔 Buffett's Logic: A consistently high gross margin signals that the company isn’t competing exclusively on price.

2: SG&A Margin
🧮 Equation: SG&A Expense / Gross Profit
👍 Rule of Thumb: 30% or lower
🤔 Buffett's Logic: Wide-moat companies don’t need to spend a lot on overhead to operate & get consumers to buy.

3: R&D Margin
🧮 Equation: R&D Expense / Gross Profit
👍 Rule of Thumb: 30% or lower
🤔 Buffett's Logic: Buffett doesn't want to own companies that need to constantly invent the next great product to do well.

4: Depreciation Margin
🧮 Equation: Depreciation / Gross Profit
👍 Rule of Thumb: 10% or lower
🤔 Buffett's Logic: Buffett doesn't like businesses that constantly need to invest in depreciating assets to maintain their competitive advantage.

5: Interest Expense Margin
🧮 Equation: Interest Expense / Operating Income
👍 Rule of Thumb: 15% or lower
🤔 Buffett's Logic: Great businesses have such wonderful economics that they don’t need debt to finance themselves.

6: Income Tax Expenses
🧮 Equation: Taxes Paid / Pre-Tax Income
👍 Rule of Thumb: Current Corporate Tax Rate
🤔 Buffett's Logic: Great businesses make so much money that they are consistently forced to pay their full share of taxes.

7: Net Margin (Profit Margin)
🧮 Equation: Net Income / Sales
👍 Rule of Thumb: 20% or higher
🤔 Buffett's Logic: Companies that consistently convert 20% of their revenue into net income are more likely to have a durable competitive advantage.

8: Earnings Per Share Growth
🧮 Equation: Year 2 EPS / Year 1 EPS
👍 Rule of Thumb: Positive & Growing
🤔 Buffett's Logic: Great companies consistently generate profits and increase them every year regardless of the operating environment.

3 Important notes:

1⃣ These “rules of thumb” are only useful when a company is mature and fully optimized for profits.

2⃣ CONSISTENCY is key. The real test is if a company generates good numbers over multiple years & various economic cycles.

3⃣ There are PLENTY of exceptions & nuances to these rules. Many of Buffett’s largest holdings do not pass every rule of thumb. That’s because investing & accounting have TONS of nuances.

text:
Liquidity vs Solvency: What's the Difference?
📚 Grab my FREE accounting infographic ebook (link in bio)

Understanding the difference is crucial for analyzing a company's financial health. 

While both concepts are related to a company's ability to meet its obligations, the terms mean different things: 

Liquidity 📊

Liquidity refers to a company's ability to cover its short-term obligations using its most liquid assets. 

This is important because a company with poor liquidity may struggle to meet immediate expenses, even if it is otherwise profitable.

Here are some key indicators of liquidity:

Current Ratio 📊
• Measures a company’s ability to pay its short-term liabilities with its short-term assets. 
• Formula: Current Assets / Current Liabilities
• Interpretation: A ratio >1 indicates that a company can cover its short-term debts.

Quick Ratio 📊
• Similar to the current ratio, but excludes inventory since it may not be easily convertible into cash.
• Formula: (Current Assets - Inventory) / Current Liabilities
• Interpretation: A ratio >1 indicates that a company can cover its short-term debts.

Companies with strong liquidity can handle short-term disruptions, but liquidity alone doesn't tell the full story.

Solvency 🏦

Measures of a company's ability to meet long-term obligations. 

A company can be liquid but still insolvent if it lacks the capacity to pay its long-term debts. 

Solvency focuses on the overall financial stability and longevity of a business.

Key solvency metrics include:

Debt-to-Equity Ratio 📊
• Compares total debt to shareholders' equity. It helps assess how leveraged a company is.
• Formula: Total Liabilities / Shareholders' Equity
• Interpretation: A ratio >1 indicates the company can is financed with more debt than equity. A ratio <1 indicates the company can is financed with more equity than debt.

Interest Coverage Ratio📊
• Shows how easily a company can pay interest on its outstanding debt.
• Interest Coverage Ratio = EBIT / Interest Expense

Total Debt Ratio 📊
• Measures the proportion of a company’s assets that are financed by debt.
• Total Debt Ratio = Total Liabilities / Total Assets

A company with strong solvency has a solid foundation for long-term growth, even if its liquidity is temporarily weak.

The Bottom Line 📌

Liquidity is about surviving in the short term.

Solvency is about thriving in the long term.

A well-run company needs both.

Cash Flow Statement Explained Simply

Follow @brianferoldi for more content like this.

Like this visual? Grab a FREE copy of my accounting infographic ebook (link in bio).
The cash flow statement tracks cash movements in and out of a business.
It provides critical information about a company's liquidity, solvency, and financial flexibility.
The cash flow statement reconciles the beginning and ending balances of cash over an accounting period.
Cash Flow Statements have three major sectors:
• Operating Activities
• Investing Activities
• Financing Activities
Here are the major categories of cash inflow & outflow for each section:
💡 OPERATING ACTIVITIES
INFLOWS
• Cash collected from customers
• Interest and dividends received
• Sale proceeds from trading securities
OUTFLOWS
• Cash paid to employees and suppliers
• Cash paid for other expenses
• Acquisition of trading securities
• Interest paid on debt or leases
• Taxes paid
💡 INVESTING ACTIVITIES
INFLOW
• Sale proceeds from fixed assets
• Sale proceeds from debt & equity investments
• Principal received from loans made
OUTFLOWS
• Acquisition of fixed assets
• Acquisition of debt & equity investments
• Loans made to others to others
💡 FINANCING ACTIVITIES
INFLOWS
• Principal amounts borrowed from others
• Proceeds from issuing stock
OUTFLOWS:
• Principal paid on debt or leases
• Payments to reacquire stock
• Dividends paid to shareholders
KEY CASH FLOW RATIOS
• Free Cash Flow = Cash Flow From Operations - Capital Expenditures
• Cash Flow To Revenue = Cash Flow From Operations / Revenue
• Cash Return On Assets = Cash Flow From Operations / Average Total Assets

It's kind of like your own personal net worth statement. It's a point in time snapshot that's taken on a specific day and it uses a cruel accounting. The balance sheet has three major components. Assets, which are everything the company owns, liabilities, which are everything the company owns and shareholders equity, which is its net worth on paper. Assets are listed in order of liquidity, which is how quickly something we can run into cash. There are two major categories. Current assets, which are expected to be used or consumed in less than a year and long term assets, which are expected to benefit the company for more than a year. There are two major categories of liabilities. Current liabilities, which are expected to be paid back in less than a year and long term liabilities, which are expected to be paid back in more than a year. Finally there shareholders equity, which is the amount of capital that investors have put into the business and the business has retained from itself. Now the balance sheet is called the balance sheet because assets must always exactly equal liabilities plus shareholders equity.

transcripts.text: Warren Buffett loves EBIT. He hates EBITDA. But what's the difference between these three things? Well, all of these stand for earnings before tax, earnings before interest and taxes, and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. They're all different ways of measuring a company's profitability with adding or subtracting certain expenses. All three of these numbers can be found on the company's income statement. Earnings before tax is also called pre tax income, simply the income that a company generates after accounting for its financing, operating, and cost expenses, but it's before paying income taxes. EBIT, or earnings before interest and taxes, is also known as operating income. EBITDA is a company's operating income plus its non cash operating expenses, depreciation and amortization. Most companies do not break these out on their income statement. To find those expenses, you have to look at the cash flow statement and specifically look at non cash charges. All of these numbers are useful when measuring a company's profitability at different ways, and they have various formulas that can be used to measure the company's valuation.

EBITDA is an acronym for Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation & Amortization.

EBITDA MARGIN
→EQUATION: EBITDA / Revenue
→Question: How much of your Revenue was turned into EBITDA?
EBITDA INTEREST COVERAGE
→EQUATION: EBITDA / Interest Expense
→Question: How many times can your EBITDA cover your Interest Expense?

→Question: How many years would it take to repay all outstanding debt if 100% of EBITDA went toward debt payments?
ENTERPRISE VALUE TO EBITDA
→EQUATION: Enterprise Value / EBITDA
→Question: What EBITDA to Enterprise Value multiple is the market valuing the company at?
PRICE TO EBITDA
→EQUATION: Market Capitalization / EBITDA
→Question: What EBITDA to Market Capitalization multiple is the market valuing the company at?

Asset vs. Equity
Assets are what the company owns and uses to generate income.
Equity is what’s left for the owners after debts are paid.

Easy reminder: Assets = Owned; Equity = New Worth.

Current Asset vs. Fixed Asset
Current Assets are short-term resources (like cash, inventory) used within a year.
Fixed Assets (like buildings, machinery) are long-term and not easily converted to cash.
Easy reminder: Current = <1 year; Fixed = +1 year.

Accounts Receivable vs. Accounts Payable
Accounts Receivable: Money owed to you by customers.
Accounts Payable: Money you owe suppliers.
Easy reminder: Receivable = Receive; Payable = Pay.

Depreciation vs. Amortization
Depreciation applies to tangible assets (like equipment) losing value over time. Amortization applies to intangible assets (like patents).
Easy reminder: D for Desks (physical); A for Abstractions (intangible).

Market Value vs. Book Value
Market Value is what someone’s willing to pay today
Book Value is what the balance sheet says the asset is worth.
Easy reminder: Market = Real price; Book = Paper price.

How to analyze a balance sheet in <2 minutes:

Answer these 12 questions:

1: How much cash does the company have?
✅ Best possible Answer: More cash than debt.

2: Are there accounts receivables? How much?
✅ Best possible Answer: None. This means the company is paid in cash.

3: Is there inventory? How much?
✅ Best possible Answer: None. This means the company doesn't have to worry about managing inventory.

4: Is there any goodwill? How much?
✅ Best possible Answer: None. This means the company has grown organically.

5: What are the company's biggest assets?
✅ Best possible Answer: Cash. This means the company has plenty of financial flexibility.

6: Does the company have debt? How much? What kind?
✅ Best possible Answer: None. This means the company hasn't financed itself with debt.

7: Does the company have deferred revenue?
✅ Best possible Answer: Yes. It's a sign that the company gets paid before it delivers the product/service.

8: What are the company's biggest liabilities?
✅ Best possible Answer: Deferred revenue. See question 7.

9: How has the company been funded? Debt? Equity?
✅ Best possible Answer: Equity. This means the company is free of debt.

10: Is there any preferred stock?
✅ Best possible Answer: No. Preferred stock is a sign that a company has poor economics.

11: Are retained earnings positive and growing?
✅ Best possible Answer: Yes. This means the company is profitable and retains its profits for growth.

12: Is there any treasury stock?
✅ Best possible Answer: Yes. This means the company is buying back stock.

Income Statement 101
What is an income statement?

It's a financial statement that shows a company's revenues and expenses over a specific period, typically a fiscal quarter or year.

An income statement provides a snapshot of a company's financial performance during that period.

REVENUES - EXPENSES = NET INCOME

The income generated (revenues) minus the costs incurred (expenses) equals the company's net income or profit.

REVENUES

OPERATING REVENUES
Sales from the company's core business operations, such as product sales or service fees.

NON-OPERATING REVENUES
Income from sources outside the core business, like interest income or investment gains.

EXPENSES

OPERATING EXPENSES
Costs directly associated with running the business, including wages, rent, utilities, and raw materials.

NON-OPERATING EXPENSES
Costs unrelated to the core business, like interest payments on loans.

TAXES
Income taxes paid by the company.

NET INCOME

The remaining profit or loss after subtracting all expenses from revenues.

Why is it important?

- Measures financial performance.
- Provides insights into profitability.
- Helps with decision-making and budgeting.
- Demonstrates the ability to generate profit.

transcripts.text: The income Statement 1:01 by Brian Furaldi. So what is an income statement? It's a financial statement that shows a company's revenue and expenses over a period of time, like a quarter or a year. So the formula is revenue minus all expenses equals net income. There are two types of revenue. Operating revenue, which is revenue from running the business, and then there's non operating revenue, and that's revenue generated from things outside of the core business, such as interest income or investment gains. And there's a few main types of expenses. Operating expenses, which are cost directly associated with running the business, and there's non operating expenses, and that's cost unrelated to the operating the business, such as interest payments on loans. Then there's also tax expense, which are taxes paid to the government. Now, why is the income statement important? Well, it helps to measure the company's financial performance, provides insights into the profitability of the business, it helps with decision making for budgeting purposes and for investment purposes, and it demonstrates the company's ability to generate profits. transcripts.text: If you're thinking about using dub app or autopilot, here's a warning for you. These platforms are rapidly gaining steam as more people want to automate their investments by copying people that they think have an edge. You see, the idea works like this. Instead of researching stocks yourself, you are replicating the portfolios of high profile investors or influencers like Nancy Pelosi in the hopes that you'll be able to replicate their success. And honestly, it's great in theory, but it has one major flaw. There is a lag between when the trade was initially made by the person and when that trade became public and your portfolio was able to copy it. And during that time lag, the price of the asset might have changed drastically. If you're late to the party and the price has already gone up before it's replicated in your portfolio, you are locking in weaker returns and taking on unnecessary risk. And all the while, the original trader has moved on to the next investment. That being said, anecdotaly, I've heard people have made some good money on it. So who knows? I'm willing to be wrong. So let me know what you think and if you've tried it.

text:
If you want to get rich in your 20s, then you need to learn from the rich people.

I went from $40k debt to a millionaire at 30, and now I'm spilling all my secrets so you can get here too.

The first thing rich people don't do is work to pay for the things they want, like the houses, cars and travel.

I just went on the most expensive vacation I've ever taken, and I didn't pay for a dollar of it out of my pocket.

Instead, I focused on buying assets like stocks and real estate that pay me while I sleep, and now that cash flow funds my lifestyle.

And this is not just "for the rich", you could buy into an apartment building for $1 by purchasing a REIT. This is one of the strategies I use, and I make 6 figures a year without working.

The second thing rich people don't do is spend time with people who don't have the life they want.

If you were trying to get sober, what do you think would happen if all your friends were heavy drinkers and spent every weekend in the bar? 

When I started hanging out with people who were making 6 figures a month, wealth became demystified. I realized when you know how money works, the amount you can make is endless.

Third thing rich people don't do is wait for shit to get bad before taking action.

Ever heard the story about how to kill a frog? 

Put a frog in boiling water, and he'll jump out right away. Put a frog in luke warm water and slowly bring it to a boil, the frog won't notice and he'll cook to death.

So many of us are in situations we say "aren't that bad", we're living paycheck to paycheck, we're in crappy jobs that don't pay our worth, we don't have money to pay our debts or buy the things we want.

Society has us in a warm water chokehold, and many people won't realize what that really means until it's too late.

text:
Today I'm going to teach you how to buy a stock.

Investing isn't for the rich, it's how you get rich, and learning how to make money while you sleep is the only way to make sure you don't work until you die.

First thing you're going to do is open an account with a brokerage - this is simply a company that gives you access to the stock market.

Then you're going to deposit money into the account, you can do this by linking your bank account and initiating a transfer.

Don't make this mistake! The account is not the investment, so if your money is just sitting there in cash, it's not growing.

To buy your investment you're going to type in the ticker symbol of the stock you want to buy. Now I don't like buying individual stocks, because no one knows which company will do the best, and we don't want to gamble with our money, so I buy investments called ETFs or index funds so I can buy little pieces of all the companies. The total stock market has gone up an average of 10% a year.

So I'd type the ticker symbol in the top, click the investment, then enter how much money I want to use. I always do a market buy (which just means buying at the price it is right now) or a fractional buy, which means buying a piece of the investment if I don't have enough for an entire share right now.

Keep learning with our Free Investing Masterclass or apply to work with me as your 7 figure mentor on our website!
