text:
This is the worker they're talking about in the video, and he says when taking the position he clarified his working hours were 9-5 est.

If this meeting is technically outside of his scheduled hours, do you think it's fair his boss expected him to be available at a moments notice to come in? 

This reminds me of the articles we've been seeing lately claiming Gen Z doesn't want to work anymore, but to me this doesn't sound like someone who doesn't want to work, but instead someone who wants to work the job and hours they signed up for.

They want to call it "quiet quitting", but I'm calling it adhering to my contract - it's like a bait and switch. You sign up for an equal exchange of services for money that everyone agreed to, and they want to change the expectations without paying it.

I think it's crazy that when you work a salary position they have no problem telling you to work overtime with no additional pay, because "you're paid for the job to get done" and youre not an "hourly employee"...

But when the job is done before 5pm you still have to stay.

These companies don't reward efficiency, they reward "optics". They'd rather you be there 10 hours a day, spending half that time walking around desk to desk with a salad in your hands, than getting the work done well in 6 and going home.

At what point do we realize that these "unwritten expectations" are more about control than anything else? 

They want to tell you what you can do and when you can do it, and they want your entire life to revolve around the business. They act like every minute task is as important as a doctor in emergency surgery. Helen, you're not saving lives you're selling office furniture, calm down.

I remember when I worked my corporate job and every month my department would be scrambling to "find the money" because the billing process for a multi billion dollar grocery chain was literally excel spreadsheets. It was always an emergency everyone had to work extra hours to correct, but it was never important enough to invest the time into building the infrastructure that would prevent this issue in the first place. It's not the workers fault that the company had inefficient policies, yet they're the ones who have to pick up the pieces when everything goes to shit over and over again.

Coming out of university my biggest aspiration was to climb the corporate ladder, until I realized the game was rigged. Sure I'd make more money, but then I'd lose even more of my time, freedom and sanity. And our generations are seeing that trade off just isn't worth it.

Instead, I learned how to invest and became financially free in my 30s. If you're ready to escape the rat race, check out our website for more.

text:
Most people stay broke not because they’re not working hard enough… but because they don’t even realize they’re trapped in a cycle.

💰 Selling tomorrow’s dollars to pay for yesterday’s spending.
💰 Keeping all their money in a savings account while inflation eats it away.
💰 Thinking the only way to make more is to work harder—while the rich make more by investing.

I went from $40K in debt to a millionaire at 30 because I learned what the rich actually do with money.

And once you see it, you can’t unsee it.

Here’s how to break out of Broke-Tok and actually start building wealth:

1️⃣ Change what you consume – If you’re constantly watching shopping hauls & “must-have” trends, you’re training yourself to spend. Wealth starts with what you feed your mind.

2️⃣ The PYF Method (Pay Yourself First) – If all your money is going to your past (debt) and present (bills), how can you ever build your future? The rich invest FIRST, so their money works for them.

3️⃣ Close the knowledge gap – Right now, you don’t know what you don’t know. The rich don’t just save—they invest, multiply, and use money as a tool. I turned $15,000 into $150,000 in 2 years because I learned how to make money work for me.

🚨 If you’re ready to start building wealth, I’m teaching my exact five-step method in my free training, From Broke to Ballin’. This is the exact strategy I used to go from $40K in debt to a millionaire by 30.

🔗 Click the link in my bio to join!

Or if you want more support? Apply to work with me as your seven-figure mentor. I’ve helped thousands of women:

💸 Pay off all their debt
📈 Start investing & grow their wealth
🛫 Travel more & enjoy life without financial stress
💍 Pay for their wedding in cash
🏡 Lock in an early retirement

Your future self is waiting—let’s make it happen. 🔥

You can't depend on anyone to take care of you in this life but yourself, and we've been lied to about what retirement is. It's not an age, it's a number in the bank.

text:
The words we we hear from our parents as children can have an impact on our belief system and the way we make decisions in adulthood.

Did you realize that by the time you were 7 years old you'd developed the rules you'd use later in life about money, based on the things we saw our parents do, say, and how they acted?

Always saw your parents fight about money?

Even the thought of money today could cause you anxiety.

Heard your parents say all rich people are a*Sholes?

You could unconsciously be scared of building wealth because you "don't want to be a bad person".

Hear your parents say phrases like "we don't have the money for that"?

It could cause a lack and scarcity mindset, which could cause you to be scared of spending money today, cause immense feelings of guilt and shame even when you spend on necessities, or could go in the complete opposite direction and cause you to overspend trying to compensate for feelings of "not having enough" as a child (even if there were).

PS. the language we use with our children matters. Instead of saying "we don't have the money for that", try saying something more specific about why. I personally love "that's not a prioirty right now", as it communicates the message that we use value based spending, and helps show children the difference between wants, needs, and tradeoff costs.

Your money behaviors today are impacted by the things we learned as children (whether intentional or not). The first step to change is recognizing the unwanted behavior or pattern, and then working to take responsibility to change them and update your belief system.

If you're looking for help learning about money and mindset, we're here to help 🤍

If you're ready to get rich in your 20s, here's exactly what you need to do, from someone who went from $40k debt to a millionaire at 30.

The first thing you need to learn is we've all been sold a lie: we're told to go to school to get a job, but then we just need the job to pay for the school. The key here is learning how to trade places with your money, so instead of you going to work to make a paycheck, your money works so you get paid while you live your life.

Understanding this helped me create a 6 figure salary for myself that I don't have to work for.

Everybody wants to know, so here's the ultimate flight hack that you need to be using!  Skip lagged! This site is so good, United Airlines sued them and lost, for providing flights that the airlines didn't want you to see.  Skip Lagged shows you hidden city airfare aka you book a multi stop itinerary but don't take the whole trip.  In this example, I wanted to take a flight from the New York city area to Dallas but the cheapest option was actually to fly from Newark all the way to Vegas and just not take the back half of the trip.  When the plane lands in Dallas, just get off the plane and leave the airport.  Follow me for more money hacks!!

transcripts.text: Surprise. Your Social Security number and data were probably just leaked again. Here's what you need to do right now to protect your money and your identity. I'm Vivian, your rich BFF and your favorite Wall Street girly. And I teach you all the finance you didn't get in school. A recently filed lawsuit alleges that back in April, cyber hackers stole the data of nearly 2.9 billion people, dead and alive, from National Public Data, the leading provider of background checks. Ironic. Hackers use your info to open up credit accounts. Then they spend money that racks up his debt under your name. And then you're left holding the bag and cleaning up the mess. Which is why you need a credit freeze to prevent any new accounts from being opened in your name. You wanna do this with all three major credit bureaus. Aquafax, Experience, and Transunion. You can call these numbers or just Google the name and credit freeze. But big key here is credit freezes are not to be confused with credit locks. Credit free services are federally mandated and free, while credit locks are sales gimmicks by the bureaus to charge you hundreds of dollars. The only inconvenience is that you'll need to unfreeze your credit the next time you apply for a loan. But in the meantime, you'll be protected. So it's worth doing.

The Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act of 1988 is a US labor law that protects employees by requiring most employers with 100 or more employees to provide a 60 calendar day heads up of planned closings and mass layoffs. All you gotta do is Google WARN act plus your state, and you'll find a DOC gov website that will show you a full list of places laying off employees. Dang, I didn't know that. transcripts.text: but only 6% of us use one welcome to part 3 of investing for beginners where I break down step by step how to get into investing so what is a stocks and shares ISA why is it the best account to invest with it's essentially a tax free investment account without you having to pay any capital gains tax or any dividend tax and some Stocks and Shares ISAs even allow you to earn interest on your cash so you don't even have to pay any tax on that you have a 20,000 pound allowance and anything you make is yours to stay untouched by HMRC the best part is you don't need to be rich to get started you can start with small amounts for example when I first started investing I started with £10 £50 here and there especially if you're young and you can set aside small amounts every month this can really snowball over time so if you want to build wealth in the UK then the Stocks and Shares ISA is probably the most powerful tool that we have follow so you don't miss out on Part 4

transcripts.text: as a financially responsible 24 year old who wants to retire by 40 these are some things that you would never see me spending my money on No. 1 is pets I don't think people realise how costly pets are until they actually get them I grew up with cats I'm such a cat person but seeing how much vet bills cost there is no way I'm gonna do that in my 20s for example we have a cat at home called Steve and he had pre existing health problems when he rescued him baby we always rescue cats but that meant that we couldn't get health insurance for him therefore he had to have like this surgery and I think it cost over £1,000 and what 20 something year old has just £1,000 to drop on an emergency medical Bill like that not many number two is a brand new car this is something that I probably won't ever buy not just in my twenties cause I know that they're a depreciating asset if I'm even going to buy like a nice car I will still probably buy it second hand because there is absolutely no point soon as you drive it out of the showroom it's gonna lose value mention the fact that in my own personal circumstances living in London there is absolutely no point other than convenience No. 3 is any designer item that costs more than my rent like that makes absolutely no sense to me I would love to own a Chanel Classic flap one day and technically I could buy one but just because I have the money it doesn't mean that I can afford to do it I'm still renting I'm still on a certain salary even though I make money from my side income it's not guaranteed I just don't feel in the financial position where I could buy it twice No. 4 is any nicotine products don't get me wrong you guys on here think I'm really boring but I have been out and about and I've done stuff for fun um all socially but I wouldn't say that I've ever got into the habit of buying these things consistently only is it such a waste of money it's so detrimental to your health that is just so much money that could go towards anything else like education self development investments No. 5 is buying the latest tech when it comes out for example the iPhone 17 only does it look kind of weird I don't feel like um there's a massive difference in iPhone upgrades currently you will not see me buying the latest iPhone just because it has like one new button those are five things that I won't be spending money on as a financially responsible 24 year old let me know what yours are in the comments below

transcripts.text: the frugal Chic who is she on the surface she appears very luxurious but underneath it all she is very savvy about her money so these are five things that characterise the Frugal Chic No. 1 she makes inexpensive items look luxurious her friends are always asking her where is this from and she says it's from vintage Zara and they're shocked she makes it look expensive it's her aura number two she walks absolutely everywhere if she can walk somewhere she will that £1 75 from the bus may not seem like a lot but that's £1 75 that she doesn't wanna spend on tfl No. 3 she has an eclectic personal style that was built over time she realises that she can't buy her way into a subculture or an aesthetic these things are curated and collected over time for example she doesn't need the latest bag charm trend she has one from five years ago from when she went on holiday the key is no one else has it No. 4 even though she loves her iced matchas iced lattes she will not be buying one every single day it's not a need it's a want she'd rather make it at home or have it at work No. 5 the frugal chic is actually not afraid to say no and she knows her values while other people call her grandma she will not be spending £400 on a night out yes she still goes out to bars sees friends at this point she's accepted that she's a little bit of a homebody but that doesn't make her boring she has other hobbies so those are five things that characterise the frugal chic do you think this sounds like you let me know in the comments below

transcripts.text: this is how to be frugal and chic you wouldn't think those two words even go together someone commented recently that I give off frugal but like quite luxury vibes at the same time that to me is like the biggest compliment because I talk a lot about how to save money and things I don't spend money on the last thing that I wanna give off is that I'm cheap here are some ways to be frugal and chic No. 1 having one signature scent one niche luxury perfume that you don't need one of those trays with a million perfumes let's be honest the amount that you probably spend on body spray various scented body creams like by the time you've done all that you could just literally buy a nice perfume No. 2 is having like a really nice lunch box either glass or stainless steel makes that frugal activity chic they definitely look better than a Tesco meal deal No.3 being an outfit repeater you would actually think that this is very unshiek wearing the same thing everyday is actually how you build personal style all of the greatest fashion icons and successful business people have all had a signature uniform that they repeat again and again okay if you're frugal and chic you know how to reuse say for example you have a dip tea candle that you've used up you're not just gonna throw that away you're gonna reuse it for cotton buds you have a designer dust bag this is gonna be used as a laundry bag when you go away if you're frugal and chic you're always thinking of ways to make things last longer than the intended purpose I think it's the ultimate flex for people to not really know what your financial situation is you turn up in the same outfit you bring your Tupperware to work but your investment account looks like this and no one else knows unless you're me and you like to overshare everything online having an emergency fund having your savings and investments all figured out that to me is a sign that you're frugal and chic

I read this book so you don't have to here's what I Learned firstly wealth is what you don't see there's that famous phrase money talks and wealth whispers and I think that's really relevant here because a lot of social media tries to convince you that the epitome of wealth is fancy cars and designer clothes but in actuality wealth is what you don't see it's your savings your investments your assets does not say that rich people don't buy nice things of course they do but one of my favourite quotes from the book is that someone with 100,000 dollar car might be wealthy but all that tells you about their wealth is that they're $100,000 less well off than when they bought the car or they're $100,000 more in debt we often gauge people's financial success based on their appearance because we don't see their brokerage account we don't see their savings another quote I really love is when people say they wanna be a millionaire what they really mean is they want to spend $1 million not actually be a millionaire another key takeaway is the man in the car paradox so the author talks about his experience being a valet driver and driving around Lamborghinis Ferraris and this giving him the aspiration to one day own one of these cars because he thought it signaled to others his wealth importance and taste the irony is he never actually looked at the drivers he looked at the cars instead of thinking wow that guy is so cool he was thinking how cool would I be if I had that car that's where the paradox comes in because we're buying these things because we want to be seen as wealthy so that we're liked and admired but often the people that you're trying to attract to admire you aren't doing so because they're only using your wealth signalling as a benchmark for their own desire to be liked and admired in summary no one is impressed by your possessions as much as you are the moral of the story here is to not stop the pursuit of wealth and the desiring of these things but to understand you only want these things because of the emotional reasons behind them you want the respect the likeability but often acquiring these things will have the opposite effect and you can achieve these things by just being a kind humble person the last key takeaway I got from the book is that nothing's free and everything has a price tag on it even if it's not immediately noticeable one of the prices that you pay for investing in the stock market is having to deal with the market volatility a lot of people say including myself invest for the long term but it's hard to invest for the long time if you're in a really bad period where your stocks are falling and you're not quite sure if they'll ever recover like most things in life the higher the returns the higher the transcripts.text: so if I'm Chinese and both my parents are white British how does that work so my parents tried to have a child naturally but it just didn't happen and they thought instead of doing IVF they would adopt at the time in China in the early 2000s they still had the one child policy what this meant was boys were the preferable gender and girls were more likely to be left for adoption this is cause boys are more likely to go out and work and also because women were seen as less important in society this meant that I was left literally on the streets of China and I was taken into an orphanage I spent some time in the orphanage but obviously it's not the best conditions even though they try to look after the kids as much as possible I was fostered for a year or a year and a half before I was adopted I think this is just to acclimatize the child to like family life I guess I think this was also a time where my parents were trying to adopt me it's a really long process and they do a lot of rigorous investigation into you as a couple to work out if you're good fit my parents got a picture of me before they adopted me I don't think they had like a choice between lots of different children I really just think it was luck growing up they always try to ensure that I was like integrated into the culture so I socialised with other Chinese girls that were adopted I also had years of Mandarin lessons but none of it stuck what I find weird as someone that's adopted Chinese and like growing up in London and everything is that there's an expectation that you should be able to do these things like people expect me to be able to speak Chinese or even things like using chopsticks like yes I am good at using chopsticks because my parents taught me but they're English but you know someone might say to me oh yeah of course you're good at using chopsticks and I'm like wait that doesn't make sense because yes my ethnicity is Chinese and I'm so proud of the way I look and the way I am however I don't feel very Chinese like where the connotations that people have with Chinese people I don't feel that I fit into that culture I feel like I'm more aligned with British culture because that's all I've known and I'm sure this is a similar experience for people that are mixed because you don't quite feel fully white and you don't quite feel fully your other culture so in that sense I sort of feel like I'm mixed but I don't have the benefits of being wasian I have been called whitewashed in the past and it's just because I don't present myself in the way that people expect like I've grown up in this really specific environment and this is just who I am and I can't really change the fact that I didn't have Chinese parents most common questions that I get asked about being adopted is no I don't know my real parents because I was left at an orphanage I don't really know who they are would I go and find them probably not because I love my parents I don't really feel like there's a part of me missing and I don't think it would solve anything in my life just because I don't look like my parents it doesn't mean that they're any less my parents I have been back to China twice one to adopt my younger sister and the other time to go back and visit my orphanage and do like a whole trip around China thank you guys for watching and if you enjoy this video give it a like and follow for more content from me

transcripts.text: these are some things I just don't spend money on as a financially responsible 24 year old who wants to retire early number one is takeaways I don't even have the delivery app or anything on my phone if I'm gonna get one I will be with friends I just won't get a takeaway because I can't be bothered to cook if you can cook really good food you just don't need to get a takeaway and also eating in the actual restaurant is so much nicer No. 2 is I don't buy coffees or sweet treats when I'm out just don't see the point of buying one every single day they're like 4 or 5 pounds sometimes that really adds up number three is I don't buy any home decor or trinkets my favourite thing to do is just collect these over time through gifts you will not be seeing me catch on to the lububu craze but these are just like sunnies angels but more demonic No. 4 is makeup and skincare I couldn't tell you the last time I tried out a new product I really just stick to the same routine of the same essential products and I just top up when they run out No. 5 is alcohol I just I'm not a big drinker if I'm out with friends I'll probably have one or two but that's it now of course I'm gonna get loads of comments saying this is so sad this is just my personal list I'm not saying other people shouldn't spend their money on these things it's just what I personally don't spend money on if you enjoyed this video give it a like and follow for more content from me

transcripts.text: okay so you've been seeing a lot of people online investing especially Gen Z and you're like I wanna get into this too I feel very behind but you just don't understand it you're scared of losing money let me explain it in such a way that by the end of this video I promise you you'll understand it let's start with the basics you have a paycheck you have cash and typically when people don't have a lot of financial literacy they think cash is king yeah I'll take even money out of a t m and I'll put it under the bed that is the best way to save so the reason why this is bad is because money every single year is devaluing because of inflation so your money has less buying power so even though you might save £10,000 if it's earning zero interest you have lost I don't know what the maths is but year on year is 3% so you psychologically don't feel like you've lost money but you actually have because you can't buy as much with that £10,000 think about Freddo's how they now cost more than they did 10 years ago so if you want to invest the reason that you would do that is because you don't want your money to earn zero interest and yes you could put it in a high yield savings account but there's different strategies that have different growth and with growth comes risk so when you invest in the stock market you're buying small pieces of company so you're buying ownership if I own shares in apple I am a shareholder you are a shareholder if you invest but when people would think about investing they typically think yeah I'll invest in apple or products or services that I use like Uber but yeah you can invest in these businesses and some of them a lot of people have made a lot of growth from investing in individual stocks but you're watching this cause you're a beginner so best tip for beginners is to not try and beat the market by trying to pick these individual stocks is actually to pick this thing called an E t F and it's an exchange traded fund what does that mean in English it just basically means this is a fund that tracks a certain list and with the stock market there's these lists of companies so say you're thinking about apple why are you thinking about that it's because it's such a large company so you're obviously going to look for one of these lists that contains the largest companies like the S N P 500 contains the top 500 companies in the U S so instead of putting all your eggs in one basket and buying apple you just buy the s N P 500 which contains apple this is what's known as diversification because even though the s N P you know that these companies serve globally because you use their products but you could also invest in an all world or global fund as well so it really depends on how high your risk tolerance is when it comes to calculated risk so a lot of people that concern is that they will lose money those disclaimers everywhere capital at risk yes it's scary as I mentioned before you have two choices either you leave your money completely in cash and it loses money through inflation or you put it in the stock market and you risk it as well what is actually the risk when it comes to investing in the stock market the risk is when you don't invest long enough the risk is when you put your money in you get scared and you take it out after a week that's when you lose money but no one that's invested for over 20 years and yes historical returns aren't a guarantee but you can look at historical trends to make a calculated risk even cash in a high yield savings account can sometimes only be protected up to £85,000 so in life there was no full proof way to completely just yeah guarantee anything so when it comes to investing that is the the two few things that you need to know about diversifying through E t F's and having a long term time horizon so it's not gonna make you rich overnight it's going to make you wealthy in the long term there's a difference so that is how to invest transcripts.text: the frugal chic who is she on the surface she appears very luxurious but underneath all she is very savvy about her money she knows where to splurge and where to save so here are five things that characterise the frugal chic No. 1 if you drive an old banger bonus points if it looks like it was handed down to you by your grandma Frugal Chic knows what an appreciating asset is and will not be financing a car until you have that £100k in the bank the Porsche can wait No. 2 she does her food shop at Waitrose and m s not very frugal but she gets yellow sticker items and also she knows the quality of these places is unmatched she'll shop their essentials line and occasionally treat herself to the higher price point items but the Frugal chic knows that there isn't too much of a difference between these shops and Sainsbury's No. 3 the Frugal chic’s makeup bag literally looks like it was pulled out of a bush every single product is used and literally about to hit pan let's just say they're well loved The Frugal chic is not wasteful makes the most of products she's also not afraid to splurge on quality frugal chic is not afraid to buy luxury but her savings come first so she uses sinking funds and a 30 day waiting rule so she's not impulse buying and over consuming and this means that she can save up for a Chanel bag but if she can't buy it twice she's not buying it at all No.5 the frugal chic best believe she is returning that parcel putting that item on Vinted the return on investment may be very low she may get £3 for a T-shirt she paid £30 for however it's the principle of decluttering her space she values minimalism and simplicity she only wants items that bring her joy do you think you're frugal chic let me know in the comments below

trading 2 and 2 which is where I have my stocks and shares ISA if you don't know what that is it's an account where you can invest in stocks and shares and any capital gains are you profit or dividends small payments from companies you make are completely tax free but most of my money is kept in here I have four pies on the platform pies are just where you can split your investments into different allocations the first one being etfs ets are essentially baskets of stocks so I invest in the S&P 500 which is the top 500 companies in the US I have what is essentially an all world fund or global fund and it's made up of developed markets and emerging markets previously I had a very low auto invest option on here now I've just set it to £1,300 because this is actually what I need to invest every month to reach my F.I.R.E number it's basically the number that I need to hear in order to live off my investments passively and you can see how close I am to reaching this goal if everything goes to plan and I keep investing this amount with the average returns I will have my fire number in 16 years next up we have my dividend stock portfolio these are just individual companies that pay you for being a shareholder as you can see the amount I have in dividend is very small at the moment but over time it's going to snowball I've got a mix of US and UK companies I've mostly tried to go for dividend kings or dividend aristocratic which have paid their difference for a certain period of time I then have a US Growth portfolio which is mostly tech stocks this is doing terribly at the moment because of everything that's going on with the market and then finally a recent addition to my portfolio is a commodities pie and this just has iShares  physical gold in it and this just tracks the price of gold this is something that I invested in at this time to sort hedge against all the volatility next we have my lifetime ISA with Hargreaves Lansdown if you don't know what a Lisa it's a government back scheme created in order to get first time buyers onto property ladder you can put in up to £4,000 every tax year and you get 25% or in this case £1,000 from the government completely free there's obviously terms and conditions that you have to be aware of before you even touch a LISA because if you withdraw and you don't meet the requirements you could get a penalty I'm personally either using it to buy my first home or for retirement in this LISA I invest in the Fidelity index world this just a global index fund then we have my workplace pension and I currently have £2,800 in here recently changed the fund that this was invested in before it was like a balanced fund and I changed it to adventurous just because I have a higher risk tolerance and I'd rather potentially get higher returns so the total comes to 78k if I was working out my net worth I'd have to take away my student loans which is about £51k we're just gonna ignore that for now but this did take me a while to build up I started with £0 and I started with very small amounts but it's just been my goal for the last five or six years to get to 100 k and I plan to do that in the next year or two so if you wanna see me try and achieve that then follow along for more

transcripts.text: how does the federal reserve raising interest rates impact inflation? let me tell you. federal reserve is raising interest rates at the fastest pace in over 40 years. this is how it can impact inflation. let's make sure we're on the same page. inflation simply means rising prices. and of course there's more to it including the consumer price index. but to understand this video just think inflation equals rising prices. and why do prices rise? well, economics 101 tells us they move up and down because of supply and demand. if you have a limited supply of something, everyone wants to buy it, then the price of that thing is going to rise, right. the people that really want it are going to pay a premium to buy it. and this is what we've seen with this over the last two years. limited supply due to supply chain issues and increased demand due to a rising economy and you have inflation. what if the federal reserve raises interest rates? by raising interest rates, borrowing money becomes much more expensive, that borrowed money is in the form of credit cards, personal loans, mortgages or auto loans, having a higher interest rate on any of those loans, means it's less affordable, which means less people and less businesses will borrow money. if less people and businesses borrow the money, that means less people are spending the money, which means demand decreases. and with their limited supply and now limited demand. federal reserve is hoping that inflation decreases. remember, there's two sides to this equation, and the federal reserve can only impact the demand side. to learn more about inflation, download the public app using the link in our bio.

First of all, let me just say the Harris proposal is limited to people with assets above $100 million. Very, very, very few people would face this tax. The tax on unrealized gains would be applied to liquid securities on an annual basis, although it would be smooth over a couple years. And then if it was illiquid private, hard to value, there'd be a set of rules that basically assume a certain rate of return, and then you reconcile when you sell it. As a tax policy nerd, this has been an idea I've been attracted to for a long time. I worry a lot about people getting locked into an investment and just holding it for the sake of not realizing their gains. I worry about all the effort people go into to borrow against their appreciated assets. And all of this can result in capital being allocated more efficiently. So as just a structural change, I like it. Um, she combines it with much higher tax rates on capital gains. I'm frankly a little bit more skeptical about that. But as a tax nerd, I like some of the neutrality that you get from this way of collecting taxes. Fewer distortions. So in for the non tax nurses out here, what do you mean in terms of, like, how does it actually create more neutrality? Like how Does it sort of even out the playing field? Right. So any tax is going to be distortionary. If you tax people on their work, maybe they'll work a little bit less on their saving, maybe they'll save a little bit less. Capital taxation is also distortionary, and I worry about that. What you want to do, though, is make it as neutral as possible so it doesn't affect decisions. You have a stock. You're deciding, should I sell the stock, should I not sell the stock? I would love you not to be thinking about taxes when making that decision. Just think about whether you're the right person to hold it. You have a company. Do you want to take the company public? Do you want to take it private again, I'd like that to be based on what is the best thing economically, not the best thing tax wise. And right now, by introducing this distinction between the taxes you pay when you sell something and when you hold something, it introduces a distortion, a non neutrality, something that can affect decision making in a way that's not productive.

India was crowned Miss Universe 2021, marking the country's first win in 21 years. But what does the winner of Miss Universe take home? For starters, let's talk about the crown. It features over 1,700 white diamonds as well as three golden canary diamonds. The massive center stone comes in at 62.83 carats.  The winner doesn't get to keep the crown at the end of her reign, but winners have been gifted smaller replica versions in the past. Miss Universe also reportedly earns a six figure salary. Back when Donald Trump owned the organization, the winners of Miss USA, Miss Teen USA and Miss Universe shared a New York City apartment, but no word on if that holds true today. The Miss Universe title comes with a modeling contract with IMG, stylist, hair and makeup artists, photo shoots, international appearances, and much more.

Costco’s pay starts at $17/hour, with  more specialized employees making around $25/hour. They also pay time and a half on Sundays, their busiest day, and offer seven paid holidays a year. Costco’s warehouse managers make an average of $114,000 a year, according to Indeed, which is better than 99% of other employers. All Costco employees get a free membership for up to four people AND a free turkey every holiday season.

transcripts.text: If you are so honored as to receive a ticket to the Met Gala, meaning you were hand picked by Anna Wintour herself, then your ticket will cost you $35,000. And if you were thinking you could bring a plus one, think again. Every single person on the guest list must be approved. And as of 2017, if you are under 18 years old you're not invited. As for the outfit, many celebrities are dressed for free by the designer, hence why so many celebs seem to, you know, ignore the theme. This is advertising for them and the designers want to show their latest designs, of course.

Six Flags is ending their unlimited food pass after TikTokers started gaming the system. They were selling an unlimited food add-on to their season pass for just an extra $80, meaning that for $200 all in, you could technically get 400 meals and 200 snacks. That comes out to just $0.33 per meal or snack if you were to take full advantage of it. And oh, were people taking advantage.  Six Flags’ CEO said the people were stuck waiting in line for up to an hour to get their food thanks to all the extra traffic from people gaming the system. They've ultimately ended the program calling it ‘highly unprofitable.’ They plan to release an amended meal plan in just a few months.

I don't know which one is worse, this or putting your burrito on a payment plan with Klarna. Look, I get it. We all need to have fun and take vacations. Even the Fed Chair Jerome Powell recently said that stocks are overvalued. So let's take a look at what we're looking at when we say stocks are overvalued. The Cape ratio or the Schiller PE ratio is looking at the prices against the inflation adjusted earnings from the last 10 years and it's sitting at a 25 year high. The only time higher was at the 2000 dot com bubble. And then we have the buffer indicator. This one simple. This looks at the total value to stock market against the GDP and this shows that the stock market is double the size of the GDP and it's sitting at all time high. text: Recent market sell-offs are largely driven by turmoil in Japan's financial markets, significantly impacting global investors engaged in the carry trade. With the Bank of Japan's negative interest rate policy, investors have been borrowing cheaply in yen to invest in higher-yielding assets abroad. However, shifts in Japanese monetary policy and rising global interest rates have led to sharp currency fluctuations and market volatility. This has forced investors to unwind their carry trades, resulting in widespread sell-offs and heightened market instability.

So remember when MacKenzie Scott and Jeff Bezos got divorced in 2019, and in the process she become a billionaire. Well she has been slowly giving away her almost $60 billion fortune, and this time she donated  $2.74 billion to charity. She wrote this blog post to say that she's donating to 286 organizations  that have been disproportionately affected by the same systems that made her wealthy. This is all part of $8.5 billion she’s already given out since July 2020, that are helping schools, nonprofits, and organizations that are helping underfunded communities.

transcripts.text: Turns out after Amber Heard’s divorce from Johnny Depp she dated Elon Musk  for nearly a year. And after yesterday's testimony, it looks like Elon Musk even made a $500,000 charitable donation in Amber Heard’s name to help her fulfill a donation pledge. Here's the backstory: Heard was granted $7 million in her divorce settlement with Depp, which she said she would be donating to charity. Half of that was set to go to the ACLU, but according to the ACLU, the payments stopped in 2018 after learning that heard was having ‘financial difficulties.’ They believe that Elon Musk stepped in to help out with one of the $500,000 payments. Musk and Heard broke up after about a year and the ACLU says Heard donated $1.3 million of the $3.5 million she had promised.

A judge has ordered Apple to pay a man a little over $1,000 USD because they didn't include one of these power adapters with his iPhone. The case took place in Brazil where a judge determined that Apple not including the power adapter was a ‘tie sale.’ This means that customers have to buy two products in order for one of them to work. Apple says they stopped including the power adapter to lessen their environmental impact, to which the judge said not so fast… you still manufacture and sell them separately. Meanwhile Apple says they still include the lightning cable and that should be enough.

text: Starting July 2026, if you own a property in Rhode Island worth more than $1 million and you don’t live there full-time, you’ll pay the "Taylor Swift tax." It will be $2.50 for every $500 of value over $1 million.

authorMeta.name: yahoofinance
authorMeta.signature: The world’s biggest business news platform: finance.yahoo.com.

transcripts.text: The Taylor Swift tax was just passed in Rhode Island. It's officially known as the non owner occupied property tax and it targets luxury second homes. They call it the Taylor Swift tax because of her seaside mansion in Watch Hill, Rhode Island, exactly the type of home that this new tax is targeting. Starting in July 2026, if you own a home in Rhode Island, it's worth over $1 million and you don't live there full time, you will pay extra. The tax will be two dollars and fifty cents for every $500 of value over that initial $1 million. In other words, a two million dollar beach house would owe roughly 5,000 extra dollars annually. There are some carve outs. If you rent out the place for more than half a year, that's 183 days, you are exempt from the tax. And by mid 2027, the one million dollar threshold will adjust for inflation. This could be the start of a new trend across the US some other states like Massachusetts, California, Maine and Montana have all floated measures targeting second home homeowners. If Rhode Island's experiment succeeds in making money without crushing its luxury market, you can probably expect other states to follow suit.

transcripts.text: A couple bought a home in Seattle, Washington only to find out it'll cost them $27,000 to access the internet. The homeowner says that all six of their neighbors’ houses are wired with Comcast, but for some reason theirs just wasn't. Meanwhile, Comcast says that they need to install 181-feet of underground cables in order to get the service up and running to the tune of $27K. In the meantime, the couple is relying on a 4G hotspot for their internet which is… not ideal. The homeowner, Zachary Cohn, says that he's been reaching out to Comcast customer service for the last eight months and they haven't been able to come to a solution.

	-TD Ameritrade

And keep watching to see where you should put your money every time you get a paycheck! 

The "Cheri Method" is a finance strategy that helps you manage your paychecks effectively to ensure financial stability and growth 

1. Savings (20%): Aim to build an emergency fund that covers 3-6 months of living expenses. 
2. Investments (10%): Invest in a diversified portfolio of stocks and bonds. 
3. Debt Repayment (20%): Prioritize paying off high-interest debts such as credit cards or personal loans. 
4. Fixed Expenses (40%): Housing, utilities, insurance, transportation 
5. Variable Expenses (10%): Groceries, dining out, entertainment 

By following the Cheri Method, you can effectively manage your paycheck, ensuring that you are saving for the future, investing wisely, paying down debt, and covering essential expenses.

The semi conductor industry is complicated and therefore often misunderstood with investors buying shares in companies without actually knowing what they do. So here's a simple breakdown. These are the companies that excel at developing advanced semiconductor chips with a heavy focus on designing the chips and outsourcing the manufacturing. Next is the IP and design arm, including companies like arm Holdings and synopsies. These are the companies that are the architects of the semi conductor world. They provide the IP and the software tools essential for chip design. The third arm of this industry is Integrated Device Manufacturers, which includes companies like Texas Instruments, Intel and Micron. These are the companies that manage both the design and the manufacturing of semi conductors which gives them a higher level of control of the entire production process but also adds more risk to the business model. And the fourth category on this list is foundries with the main company being Taiwan Semiconductors. They exclusively produce chips that are designed by other companies like in video and AMD. transcripts.text: If no one's actually ever told you how to save money, this is a step by step, foolproof guide to give you guys some background. I started saving with very small amounts like £50, £100. Don't get discouraged about seeing other people's larger amounts, because those tiny amounts at the start, they're really what gets the ball rolling. And anything that you can put aside is an achievement. No. 1 know your income. If you're employed full time, take a look at your payslip. It's important to not just know your salary, but what your take home pay is after pensions, national insurance, and tax is taken off. No. 2 is track your spending. Now you don't need to restrict yourself, it's more about being aware of what you're spending. I feel like the easiest place to start is literally getting a pen and paper and writing down what your expenses are. Rent, bills, grocery. And literally see how much you spend on a typical month. If you wanna make things easier, I really recommend using a budgeting app like Emma. Links with your bank account so it can literally show you the insights of what you're spending. For example, it will tell you if you're spending £200 on transport. Number three is use a budgeting rule at the start. Take the 50 30 20 rule for example. and 20% to your future. It might be that when you start Your future category is only gonna be made up of 5 or 10% or even less. If you wanna change those percentages later, it's completely up to you. Number four is know your goals and separate them. For example, you've got long term saving and investing. This is like for the next 20+ years. Then you have things like your emergency fund and they usually 3 to 6 months worth of living expenses. You will then have other short term savings like holidays, Christmas. These are all things that are really good to budget and save for ahead of the time so that you don't have to use say a credit card and then go into debt. It also helps to even out your expenses. You're not just randomly spending 4 hundred pound extra at Christmas. No.5 is have a clear vision. Don't just say you want to save, you need to get pen and paper and write down how much you want to save. I don't care how delusional you think it is. Then it's not even about the number. You have to have an emotional reason of why you want to hit this number. Is it that you want more time to spend with family? Is it that you're in a toxic job? Or you don't want the financial stress of all your decisions being about money? Final step would be to automate your savings, ensuring that you have a direct debit set up to a high Yield savings account. A cash ISA or stocks and shares ISA. Whatever you choose to do, but make it unconscious. Make it like a Bill and set it on the day that you get paid with the amount that you can afford to put aside. This is really a game changer. So that is a step by step tutorial of how to save. I hope that you found this useful, and if you did, give it a like and follow for more content from me.

transcripts.text: so you wanna start investing but you need someone to explain it to you as if you're 5 years old don't worry I've got you if you're new here my name is Mia I make personal finance and investing simple for beginners if you wanna see more content from me then follow along for more investing in the global stock market means you're buying small pieces or shares of companies all over the world and when you're a shareholder you're essentially a part owner of that company if the company grows and makes more money and the value of their share price goes up which is driven by many factors then the value of your investment goes up with it you can then sell these shares for profit and that's what's called capital gains some companies even pay you a small reward for holding their shares and this is called a dividend and it's paid to you in cash so those are the two ways that you can make money in the stock market either by selling your investments for a profit or by getting a dividend so don't let that fool you into thinking it's just fun and games you've probably seen many disclaimers saying capital at risk and the fear of losing money is probably one of the biggest reasons why people don't invest you've probably seen those graphs of stocks swinging up and down and this is called market volatility if you're invested in something like a high growth tech stock this is going to be more volatile than a blue chip dividend stock like Coca Cola blue check just meaning it's very valuable just the same way you would have in a poker game those are two examples of different investments that you could have stock prices can go up and down depending on many factors like the company's performance the economy and investor emotions but your main concern is probably what happens if my investments go down so the way the stock market works is when you have your investment it might go up or down in value but you haven't gained or lost any money until you actually realise those losses or gains and the way you would do that is by selling whether you sell out a profit or whether you sell out a loss until then your gains and losses are on paper to reduce risk of losing money you can do two things No.1 would be to diversify and that's when they invest in multiple things to spread out the risk of their investments the easiest way to do this is to invest in an ETF which is a basket of stocks it's much less risky to invest in 500 stocks all at once and to put all of your money in one and the second easiest way to reduce risk is to have a long time horizon if you're invested in a passive ETF and you wait over 15-20 years you could reduce your risk to 0.1% so from all of this it's safe to say that investing is really for the long term what does that tell you leave the day trading to the professionals and just focus on having a long term passive strategy markets that you can invest in have generally risen over time therefore patience is key if you enjoy this video give it a like and follow for more past finance and investing content from me

transcripts.text: this is how to actually sell digital products as a side hustle this is how much I've made in the last few months and I know it's not a crazy amount but this is a realistic guide for people wanting to start so firstly the platform that I use is gumroad other people might like to use Etsy but Etsy charge you per listing gumroad is completely free but they'll take a fee once you make a sale so you basically start by making an account after you've done this you actually need to have a product to sell I would use platforms like Canva which is completely free or word or Excel to make digital products probably going to want to have some social media page or blog to drive traffic to your products you really wanna focus on things that are actually useful and helpful for people so things that you use yourself so if it's a budgeting template or even if it's a recipe something that you find useful share with other people don't just make digital products with the hopes that you're gonna make money because of course that is the end goal if that's your only goal then you're not going to be very successful you have to actually think what's relevant to your niche once you make your dish product you just upload it to download the next step is really marketing if you are a content creator or just someone wanting to find a side hustle then this is a really good one because there's no offering costs there's no inventory uh other than the fees that get taken away from the sale it is completely free let me know if you have any questions in the comments below and follow for more content from me

transcripts.text: I am addicted to saving but I feel like that's why I have 120 k saved at age 24 so here are the different ways I hacked my brain into saving No. 1 I treated it as a competition between me and consumerism every time I didn't buy something I won we are so bombarded with marketing everywhere on our phones when we go outside even shopping now is considered a hobby if I got the temptation to buy something that I just did not need and I waited I didn't buy it I saw that as an achievement because it's almost like I outsmarted the marketing No. 2 is I got a dopamine hit every single time I saw that number go up even at the start like when I had a couple hundred pounds in savings even seeing it go from 500 to 600 know when you invest it's actually better to not look at your account but I found the opposite I prefer to look at it daily even if it's fluctuating down or up seeing that number go up through contributions or capital gains that's what gave me motivation No. 3 is I actually made it my goal to get rich and a lot of people don't want to admit this to themselves because they think it's greedy or evil what you really want if you want this is financial stability the difference is between a lot of people is that they want to spend like a rich person but they don't actually want to be rich because that would take a lot of work therefore making that distinction between wanting to spend or live like a rich person versus actually being a rich person or doing the habits that a rich person would have those are three mindset shifts that I had to make to get to where I am if you enjoyed this video give it a like and follow for more content from me

here are my rules for my low by year going into 2025 unlike a no by year where you literally can't buy anything non essential a low by year is slightly less strict and I think it's more achievable for most people so here are some rules that I'm going to try to follow from my low by year take inspiration if you think it applies to you starting with No. 1 Project Pan this is where you try to use up every single product to its last drop what this involves is squeezing out every last product cutting it open to get the last bits out and you may think oh who can be bothered to do that but it's really important we waste so many products year on year and so many products go into the bin expired and unused No.2 is eating out and coffees are treats so I've always done this in my budget I do think that eating out and coffees should be treated as something special and a treat if it becomes an everyday thing it's not only a really bad financial habit to get into because it's gonna cost you a lot but also you're gonna appreciate those things a lot less No.3 is second hand first what I mean by this is always look for something second hand before you buy first of course this doesn't apply to things like underwear or makeup or anything like that but anything that you can buy second hand I would always recommend looking for it first because not only will you save a ton of money it's also much better for the environment number four is wait 30 days before buying that thing that you want I recommend making a list on notes and just writing down when you started wanting it and check back a month later number five is sell them buy what I mean by this is try and sell your old stuff and use that money to buy new things if you're like me and you're on your journey to building your capture wardrobe or your forever wardrobe a lot of the things that you might wanna buy are expensive because they're investment pieces so this is a good way of raising that capital so that you don't feel as bad splurging No.6 is I'm allowed to invest in quality as a last point suggested I'm actually happy to spend a lot of money on things I know I'll wear forever No. 7 is stay low maintenance this includes my hair my nails I don't do anything um at a salon because No. 1 I hate the appointment booking process and also when you're there it feels like such a waste of time and then sometimes when they get it wrong it's like it's the worst feeling going to pay and paying £40 for something that you don't even want No. 8 is no shopping apps not keeping any shopping apps on my phone this is gonna stop the temptation from scrolling on them as if their social media No. 9 is drugstore products this includes skincare or makeup this doesn't include if it's something really special that I know I'm gonna use for the whole year like my way shampoo that tends to last me about a year but anything else I use up quickly like a face wash I will just get from the drugstore or even a supermarket No.10 is travel and experiences are always allowed I think travel and experiences are always worthwhile spending money on because you'll remember those for the rest of your life as opposed to a material object that on your deathbed you're not going to be thinking about so those are my rules for my low buy year going into 2025 I'll keep you guys updated if I manage to stick to it if you enjoyed this transcripts.text: there is no bigger flex than a woman that has her own finances sorted. a couple years ago, I kind of got sucked into that whole world of hypergamy creators like Sarah 7, who I think is very entertaining, but that's what she is, an entertainer. this kind of rhetoric of chasing a soft life is very attractive. at the end of the day, that's all we want. freedom to kind of go to Pilates, get a matcha and have a nice time. we all want that. something that I learnt very early on in life is nothing is free. when you're financially dependent on someone, they have a say in what you do. it's like when your parents pay for your wedding, they then get a say on how it goes. and I do believe as women, we offer so much emotional labour, domestic labour, all of these different things. therefore we should be dating people that bring value to our lives. there's no doubt about that. feel like as I entered my mid twenties, but 2 I became the most financially literate I had been. and as my income doubled in the last year, I kind of realised what it felt like to have my own money. of course I already had an income, but actually make enough money where I felt financially free. that was a different feeling. almost feel like this chasing of a soft life or thinking that you're gonna get it through. a man often comes because you feel a lack of financially. if you had your finances savings in order, you probably wouldn't feel that way. if you're still in this mindset that someone else is going to do it for you, prepare for a life where you get assigned values and tasks. you trade one boss for another. I get it. the world of finance investing can seem overwhelming and like it's not meant for us. honestly, the internet has democratized this information. I urge you to take a few hours to just learn about the basics. stocks and shares, ices, emergency funds. these are all things that we should be knowing about as women. yes, it's fine to want a rich man, but I think we can also be rich women ourselves.

transcripts.text: here's a step by step tutorial of how to invest in the S&P 500 and the FTSE ALL world on the trading 212 because last time I made this video it got deleted so I won't be including any screenshots I'm just going to be talking about it just a disclaimer this is not financial advice and when investing your capital is at risk the first thing I recommend you doing is opening a stocks and shares ISA this takes literally five to 10 minutes you need your National Insurance number and you need to confirm you're not a US tax resident and all of these various things and once you've done that you've read the terms and conditions you can open your stocks and shares ISA the reason you want to open a stocks and shares ISA and instead of using the invest account is because you won't be taxed on capital gains or dividends um the allowance for capital gains and dividends in the general investment account is £500 for dividends and £3,000 for capital gains this is not something that you want to be keeping track of in the long term if you are investing for the long term you want it to be in an ISA so that you don't have to declare these taxes or capital gains to the government so if you didn't know you've got a 20 k allowance of how much you can deposit into various ISAs that's a stocking shares ISA a cash ISA a lifetime ISA and the various different ISIS it's up to you to keep track of how much you're putting in each and make sure you're not going over the 20 k threshold so when typing in the SMP 500 I think the first two that pop up are Vanguard etfs and both of them are different strains of technically the same ETF difference between them is that one is accumulating and one is distributing so you'll probably see two Vanguard Etfs one of them is VUAG and this is the accumulating version of the fund and visa the USA and this is the distributing version of the fund be wondering why they have these weird names and this is just an easier way of identifying the fund instead of having to say the full name think of it as a little nickname for the fund it's highly recommended for beginners and long term investors to pick the accumulating version countless amounts of research has proven that people that choose the accumulating version make more money over the long term so the charges if you want to check them out you can go into the page of the ETF and scroll to the bottom and look at the key information document this basically comes from Vanguard and this tells you about the ETF and it tells you about the risk um equities are a high risk asset class and that's why there are um disclaimers and there's warnings against this if you are investing money that you might need in the next five years it's probably recommended that you don't invest in this because if you have to sell at an awkward time when the markets down you are going to lose money so check out this key information document it's got a risk um it's got a risk level of about 6 out of seven um scroll to the bottom you will find the charges the charges for the UAG and visa are 0.07 so they're very very low and that's because this is the most passive you can get with investing it's just a tracker fund and it tracks the top 500 companies in the US so if you were thinking about investing in the SMP 500 and the Allworld Fund which is its own video it's a debate about whether you need both of them but if you do want to have both of them you can make a pie and I recommend making a pie because then it sort of keeps the certain waiting that you've decided to say you want to keep 7% in the SMP maintain that waiting for you so you don't have to work out manually pies are also great because you can also reinvest so it can take money out of your free cash that you've got in the account and reinvest it and you can do this every week or every month and this is actually a method called dollar cost averaging which is known as a really tried and true method of investing for the long term because you're investing regular amounts at regular intervals so I highly recommend that you set this up and automate it as much as possible this bit is really important so listen carefully if you want to do the pie strategy you really want to make sure that you're not buying into the etfs outside of the pie this will just confuse things because you will look at your portfolio on the front page and it will say that you have a certain amount of shares then when you go into the pie it will be a different value and it will just be awkward trying to sell and it will just get confusing so make sure you go into the pie and click on your holdings and press invest and buy the funds through the here this is a much better way because it when using the pie feature it will balance your portfolio for you based on the allocation that you set if you buy outside of the pie it will will not be able to keep track of how much you bought outside of the pie so that's how you buy the SMP 500 on trading 2 1 2 I particularly recommend trading 2 1 2 on its own like as a platform I use it but I'm not making that as a recommendation I think Vanguard and other platforms are equally as good it's up to you to do your own research and find the appropriate one for you as always if you enjoyed this video give it a like and follow for more personal finance and investing transcripts.text: one of my biggest financial goals is to get to 100 k in my savings and investments and that's because famous investor Charlie Munger once said that getting to your first 100 k will be the hardest hurdle in your journey to financial freedom and that's because before you reach this number you're literally starting from zero and most of the growth in your net worth is coming from deposits from your earned income after this stage once you reach 100 k compound interest starts to become a lot more visible in your portfolio and starts to snowball and also the returns that you can get on your investments could actually outpace the amount that you're able to deposit so I thought it'd be fun to see how close I am to reaching this goal and by the way I'm not making this video to brag or make anyone feel bad about their own finances everyone has different circumstances and I just love sharing my journey for anyone that's interested so to start in my general investment account which is where I hold short term savings and any money that I can't put in my ISA £6,369 and for the majority of my savings and investments in my stocks and shares ISA I have £68,899 and then for my lifetime ISA which recently got the 1,000 pound boost from the government this is coming to 17,476 pounds the last video I did like this I didn't count my workplace pension but I would say it sort of counts this is coming to 2,400 pounds so the grand total of all of my savings and investments is £95,144 which is insane it doesn't even feel real and I'm sure it'll feel even weirder to reach the goal one thing to know is I have to pay some of this in taxes that will be in January and I feel like by the time I get there I may even hit the goal I do genuinely think it's because I'm focusing on transcripts.text: so I've gained quite a few new followers recently so I thought I'd do an updated get to know me so the first question that I always get asked when I meet people in person or just online is where are you from I always say London typically southeast London or Lewisham and I pretty much lived there my whole life until recently I moved out in February the next question is always where are you from originally well I'm from China I am from Wuhan which obviously has an amazing reputation but basically I am adopted so my parents are British hence the accent whatever reason they couldn't have kids they decided to adopt and at the time there was a one child policy I don't know if that was exactly why I was adopted because I don't know birth parents or anything I was literally left on the streets outside of the orphanage I actually went to school in Croydon I was brought up Catholic and even though I'm not practicing now I think it gave me a lot of good values I was sent to a specific Catholic school in Croydon but I know what you're thinking Boyden and Lewisham I must be very street wise so even though I don't believe in god I am very interested in religion and philosophy so for a levels I did religious studies English lit and history you may be thinking where is this leading to how does it relate to fashion or stock no idea what I wanted to do at university I was originally thinking of doing ancient history I didn't really know where that would leave me career wise so it was actually my mum that found the course was fashion management and I went to do this at Nottingham Trent cause I wanted the whole uni experience sadly a lot of my uni experience was affected by Covid regardless I still think it was such a good experience which leads me on to my next point what do I actually do as my full time job so I work in the fashion industry but I actually work a fashion showroom so we wholesale premium brands to retailers so it's business to business instead of direct to consumer I personally work on the sustainable footwear brand VEJA my official title is an account manager working in fashion definitely isn't for the faint hearted it's not glamorous and you are working really hard and surprisingly doing a lot of manual labour sometime but I do enjoy it I do go to a lot of things like Paris Fashion Week as for how I got into finance as a hobby I had two male friends at university and they were showing me their portfolios one of them like their parent had set up for them it was mostly an index funds and the other one was like actively trading individual stocks this just immediately got me interested it felt like a little boys club that I was not allowed to be in so that obviously made me want to learn about it more so I took to reading books like Rich Dad Poor Dad psychology of money really immersed myself in this topic watched Youtubers like AndreI Jikh who used to do a lot of like dividend stock videos back in the day and he's just like my favourite Youtuber ever it's also at university that I got into modelling I was scouted by Instagram after not having it for a few years worked with brands like Jd sports the hip store I don't really do it too much anymore I don't know why like I'm super busy with work and with the modelling industry you have to take a lot of time to go to castings do self tapes and stuff and it's just something that I have no capacity for but I actually only started posting content fairly recently it was last June that I posted my first ever TikTok and I never saw myself as a Tiktoker I never thought that I'd be like talking to the camera or anything cause I'm naturally quite a shy person first video got like 50 k views and I guess that prompted me to keep going so some random facts to finish I'm a Sagittarius my favourite t V show is The Walking Dead I'm obsessed with anything zombie related I have three cats at home James Peter and Steve they all have middle aged man names I like reading and I also love cosy games like Stardew Valley and even though I'm not an expert in it I'm a self proclaimed cinephile so I love rating films on letterbox that's me in a nutshell I feel like I don't share too many other sides of myself apart from the finance side but these are just a couple of little facts about me
